claim: Says she joined SM as a design graduate interested in record-cover work, reasoning that the best-known label of the time would be an interesting place to work in several senses.
Describes her own listening history as far from idol pop: world music, bossa nova, jazz, disco, punk, AOR, French pop, lounge — chosen by a firm personal style regardless of nationality or genre.

Defines creative direction (in her SM context) as giving visual form to the imagery a piece of music evokes — making a 'visual fantasy' concrete — and as overseeing artwork, styling, music-video planning and production and pre-release teaser promotion, building the artist's image beyond the usual categories of design or video.

Names promotion devices as part of the creative work: an exhibition event before f(x) '4 Walls', an EXO 'EXODUS' passcode promotion run as a deduction game with fans, treating the EXO symbol as a brand identity varied album by album, and a SHINee colour-chip promotion.
Says the industry had no such role or department when she joined, which is why the work felt meaningful, and that she intends to keep its scope unconstrained, planning flexibly from a visual basis.
Describes the SM corporate identity she directed as a 'flexible identity': a brand system built to transform and extend so the company could respond to many content types and media as it expanded.
Argues that culture increasingly prioritises the visual, i.e. intuition, and that in K-pop visuals are effectively equal to music and act as a catalyst.
Says that rather than trying to meet every culture's beauty standard she emphasises each team's individuality.

Rejects the idea that she seeks difficulty on purpose; says she is interested in essence and newness. For SHINee's 6th album she used primary colours and basic shapes that even children know, and reread the group's name ('light') as 'the one who receives light', choosing colours that signal permanence.

Argues that a physical album worth collecting in the digital era should be treated as a different kind of object; whether a cover shows a face is the wrong question — the cover's own symbolic role is the point, especially when the package already contains enough portraits.

On the 'factory-made K-pop' critique: in a saturated, capital-rich idol market anything new is immediately mass-reproduced until it is unclear who did it first; she frames this as a broader problem of an era where money justifies anything, requiring individual reflection plus collaboration.

Advises would-be art directors that the market is oversaturated and highly developed, that a genuinely different breakthrough is needed, that complacency means falling behind, that newness must keep being pursued, and that authenticity and a firm core matter more as things get harder.

Says SM's music was far from her own taste (she grew up on international LPs and film soundtracks, jazz-based European and world music), and that this distance made joining interesting: the company was far from her but close to the public. Trained in popular art, she wanted to communicate with the public through inspiring rather than disposable graphic work; cites Hipgnosis as a formative influence; expected that realising her intentions through the specialised 'idol' genre would be ironic and thrilling.

Recalls that early on few people at SM understood the link between concept and graphics or how materials should derive from a concept; managers separately outsourced shoots, design and styling. The hardest part was building the organisation, which took longer than expected and required patience and careful strategy.
Describes a large organisation as a living but slow-moving rock; moving it flexibly requires persistence, and small moments accumulate into major change.

Names a TVXQ Christmas album as her first 'systematic' project: a 'gift' logic in which members exchange gifts secret-Santa style and the album itself is defined as a gift to fans, which fans could in turn give to others; the same logic governed concept, shoot, set and design.

Says that at Girls' Generation's launch, on hearing the group name, she made an image map and briefed the producer on the cover concept and overall visual direction, arguing that the crux was what kind of 'girl' and how 'girl' would be expressed; the producer asked that it be shared with all team leads, and her remit then widened step by step (stage costumes came later).
Describes her job as planner, visual maker and sometimes marketer, a role that did not previously exist; wants to do work that is both necessary and fun.

Calls SHINee's 'Romeo' the album that most fully realised her intention: she proposed the title, was exacting about photographer casting (even considered shooting it herself because the key was a subtlety hard to explain), deliberately chose photographers doing unfamiliar work rather than mainstream names, and offered them a free method after explaining intent and purpose. Says mismatched pairings are more interesting and the major/underground boundary is meaningless if purpose and result are met.
Says she dislikes scattered work without a centre and sees her role as a kind of storyteller.
Cites an exhibition of the publisher and art director Robert Delpire as a significant source of renewal in a difficult period of work.
Says SHINee and f(x) projected images she had long imagined ('wouldn't a group with this image be interesting?'), and that the satisfying moment is when that idea meets the members' individuality.

Answering criticism that SHINee/f(x) concepts are hard to read: the single goal is whether the intended message got through; she tries to communicate with the public without damaging the purpose, accepts that not everyone can be made to understand, but does not ignore accessibility either — it is a tightrope between the centre that must be kept and the gap.

For EXO, wanted to bring out the members' coexisting sexiness and freshness from debut; hearing 'Growl' suggested school uniforms; she translated the earlier 'wolf' motif indirectly (wolf → masculinity → a boy's passion) and told the story of a boy in love inside a 'school' concept, plainly and honestly.

On running her team: does not impose overtime, expects people's best within their own time, allows working from home and late starts, and wants a playground-like company; observes that many people struggle with flexible ways of working.
In 2013 describes SM as an earnest, more human organisation than outside descriptions of a 'music factory' suggest.
Names her priority as not being trapped by fixed ideas and keeping flexible thinking, because complacency kills the fun.

In a 2016 lecture said that before SM she had little interest in popular culture, without chasing obscurity either, but had a firm personal style; joined because putting her influence into work many people see seemed interesting, and approached each project simply by trying to make it satisfy herself.

Says the f(x) 'Pink Tape' art film was technically modest by design: the aim was not craft but to set an image standard for f(x); she asked what would be fun and what would not feel contrived, hoping it would be welcomed and help the company.

Says she had a plan for what f(x) should be from the start but its realisation fell short; since she could not replace people, she took a 'second-best' route that harmed no one — a fun, ultra-low-budget side project.
Says f(x)'s launch coincided with her gaining rank and a voice at the company, at a time when few employees offered opinions; she used it.
The Pink Tape art film was reportedly made on a real production budget of about KRW 5 million with film-student collaborators.

On f(x) '4 Walls' after a member left: re-imaging the group as a quartet was hard; the work had to compensate for the loss of a 'visual' member and make the group read as solid rather than visual-led, and the promotion had to be made fun.

Says she disliked SM's music videos and wanted them to change, which is why she worked inside the organisation rather than as a freelancer; adds that creative work in the Korean idol market carries many constraints.

For f(x) 'Red Light' she expanded the lyric's 'warning' into the idea of deviating from what everyone holds to be true, putting opposites (good/evil, utopia/dystopia, taboo/desire) in one frame; argues 'objectivity' is an accumulation of subjectivities; aim was to show a differentiated f(x) philosophy amid a flood of predictable idol groups.
Says good visual work does not just get music heard; it maximises synaesthetic imagery.

Describes moving deliberately between friendliness and unfriendliness toward the audience, stopping short of the point where the public finds it too unfriendly; easy things are easy to make and work but tire quickly and are not interesting; meaningful work that is slightly unfriendly is good work.
Says she likes the expression 'visualising music' and regards it as close to performance art.

On Girls' Generation's 'Black SNSD' (Run Devil Run): the concept was discussed months in advance; it was meant to show a more powerful femininity while keeping the group's innocence, not 'sexy'; she chose covering the body over exposure, using lines that suit the members, and said that if sexiness is measured by exposure the concept has none.

Explains that the biggest change was a single signature detail per member (e.g. one member's first-ever bangs, another's hair moving from innocent to mature), with uniform-like group outfits mixed with individually suited ready-to-wear on a black base.
Says the emotional effect multiplies when a fan can hold an object from an artist they like while listening to it and also receive a visual shock.

Says she sets the styling concept from the first image a song evokes: 'Gee' suggested early-1980s film-star casualwear (white T-shirts with jeans or coloured skinny jeans); 'Tell Me Your Wish' a uniform; 'Oh!' a cheerleader.
projects: Girls' Generation Tell Me Your Wish

claim: Names a fashion-show finale, where models in different garments gather in one scene, as the reference for Run Devil Run, and states that 'healthy girl' is the unchanging base principle of Girls' Generation's concepts.
Says consumers meet music first through the CD cover and that a CD is now something to look at rather than listen to.

For Girls' Generation 'The Boys', the jacket expressed the group's mood lyrically through fairy-tale princess characters, while the stage pushed a stronger, dignified princess image suited to the song — one idea with different intensity per channel.

Explains SHINee's 'Dream Girl' as not simply a woman: people seek an ideal who resembles or is opposite to them, which is a search for another self. With all members now adults she wanted a more serious side, letting photos carry what cannot be said directly; the jacket photos are the members' fantasy — both the woman they seek and themselves.

Says SHINee's albums have been shot with underground photographers and photographers' assistants who have sense and understand the planner's intent, whereas idol peers favour fashion photographers; SHINee leans toward the 'minor', on the view that fresh art grows from a minor base.

Rejects trend-chasing: styling is 'what we like'; since clothes of the moment are what exist, you follow trends anyway, but trying to get ahead of them is childish. Defines a trend as what the public naturally copies when someone does something that looks right; her test is whether a style suits the members, looks good, and makes others want to follow.

Values unplanned on-set improvisation (a member's coloured eye make-up, a choker customised on the spot because a tie would not suit the outfit); such accidents produce something uniquely theirs, which becomes the group's colour and, if liked, a trend.

Does not choose staff for fame; wanted to build SM's own team, e.g. hair and make-up staff who had never styled singers, because people who worked with other singers carry the past with them; fresh work can come from students; amateur or not, work with fresh, interesting people, and surfacing them can develop the industry.

Calls the whole cycle — album production, the group's performance and the public's listening — a kind of performance art; is not bound by others' judgements but thinks creating a discourse everyone can enjoy matters, and wants albums to put a topic into popular culture.
Reported to have proposed SHINee's album theme 'Misconceptions', on the idea that beautiful misunderstandings make the world beautiful and life interesting.
Rejects the 'boy becomes man' cliché; frames each album as a 'growth report' documenting how the members change over time, with this album marking a turning point because all members were now adults.

Prefers that artists enjoy the process rather than chase set targets, arguing that attitude matters as in fashion: honesty plus diligence, and showing the present state well, is what reads as attractive.

Explains the two chapters of SHINee's 'Dream Girl' as 'misconception about you' and 'misconception about me': chapter one hid faces, chapter two erased them; the unreadable face stands for SHINee as each viewer sees them.

Describes SM opening collaboration shops with four Korean fashion brands as an unusual pairing of SM with subculture, which in turn produced remix albums pairing SM artists with Korean hip-hop and indie musicians.

Says the EXO collaboration shop was deliberately not aimed at general customers; prices followed from the makers involved; the product range was intentionally narrow (planned as only coats and knits) and widened only in response to demand.

Reported: the shop ran with no advertising, relying on social word of mouth, and with low investment. She says that although art direction is not the business side, she had long wanted to do something commercially interesting — to stop commissioning stage costumes and taking brand sponsorship and instead create revenue through a new business.
Frames the shop as growing together with emerging Korean designers who have talent but lack capital and promotion, noting rising overseas interest in Korean design.

Says entertainment differs fundamentally from manufacturing — nobody can know in advance how an act will perform in a new market — and explains the collaboration as 'corporate asset management': using existing resources to cut costs (making artists' clothes in-house) while adding income by selling them to the public.
Summarises Red Velvet's debut concept as 'vitamin', taken from the debut song's lyrics; tropical-palm imagery in the album art and video came from the jungle-like sound of the beat.

Explains Red Velvet's debut styling as minimal preppy outfits with loud accessories and primary colours; each member's hair colour followed her character, chosen to make new members distinguishable while adding a jungle-like funkiness.

Explains f(x) '4 Walls' stage styling: restraint to suit voguing choreography; 1970s silhouettes mixed with contemporary feeling to express a dance that is at once dynamic and flexible; the stage continued the artwork and video concept, e.g. covering dancers' eyes for a mysterious, dramatic tone, so that sleek EDM would feel unfamiliar and intense.
Describes SHINee's uniforms in the 'Everybody' era as a symbol of leadership derived from the keyword 'Everybody'.

Says she did not particularly enjoy the K-pop scene during her long time in it; the work was often painful and her focus was on how to do it better. She founded ADOR to do fully what she wanted as a creative director inside a company whose direction might otherwise differ, not out of a wish to pioneer.

Explains NewJeans' expected success not as confidence in her own skill but as respect for consumers: if a product fills what the scene lacks, and does so together with other areas, consumers will recognise the alternative.
Says the year before NewJeans' debut left her no personal life: daily thinking and review, which is where her confidence at launch came from.
Says many people, including self-described experts, told her NewJeans' kind of music could not reach number one or appeal to overseas fans, which made her want to show otherwise.
Argues the public cannot like only one direction; her approach was to chase what she found interesting without dictating, expecting others would find it interesting too.

Says she did not deliberately target global fans when making music videos: with YouTube, everyone has become a neighbour, and universal human emotions mean that well-made points of empathy will be enjoyed abroad too.
Warns against reducing K-pop's appeal to a single factor, while suggesting that earnestness and sincerity in how Koreans approach work comes through to audiences.

In a 2026 interview (Kim Hye-ri, '조용한 생활') says that at SM she was a producer who did not put herself forward: despite attention and requests (including TV and advertising offers from her mid-thirties) she declined them all, preferring to stay in the creative-director role.
Says she likes mixing completely different designs and enjoys the mysterious harmony they produce; she shaped her home to her own way of living rather than fitting herself to a typical interior.
Describes Seoul's appeal as mountains and water inside the city and the coexistence of plain, unadorned traces of earlier times with very rapid change.

Says ooak records should not confine itself to music: with artists and music at the centre, different kinds of creative work should connect and extend freely; describes the Casa BRUTUS project as linking Seoul's spaces with fashion and design.
The Casa BRUTUS project extended into a collaboration with the Japanese fashion brand everyone, producing 'everyone ok' caps and T-shirts using the Hangul word '오케이', launched through a pop-up.

OOAK's launch released 23 campaign videos at ten-minute intervals (about 3h50m in total), placing an 'ooak record shop' in ordinary street scenes of many world cities, ending in Seoul, with recruitment notices and clues about a first boy group hidden as easter eggs.
States that the essence of entertainment is raising quality of life through small everyday happiness, and that she will plan the boy group in line with that, with sincerity as a producer.

The label described the campaign as rejecting the industry's typical one-way promotion in favour of short bursts that keep stimulating the public to find answers; she said she wants to surprise with creative work and a business style not seen in the existing entertainment market.

OOAK's channels opened without prior notice; the website showed a face turning into a bird with a whistle; a date-only 'coming soon' post and apparel printed with the launch time preceded any explanation.
She announced the new company on her own account with drawings and doodles rather than a corporate release; the name ooak stands for 'one of a kind', also glossed as 'only one always known'.

Names her own taste and sincerity as what matters most in creative work: wholehearted effort toward the goal, for the artists or for herself, which is invisible and formless but which she believes reaches fans.

Argues that what people like and are instinctively drawn to does not change across eras — like children's private 'treasures' — and that she wants to make things that never grow old and are good whenever seen, works that stir imagination.
Says that in entertainment, once a hit formula appears it is repeated until everyone's style converges, and that she wanted to break this.
Says she wanted NewJeans' members to look like their actual age — unselfconscious and bright — and to make content that is not uniform and provokes as much curiosity as possible.

Says she wanted a group with a natural atmosphere — matching the era, differentiated from existing styles and her musical direction — and that realising everyday naturalness is hard: it requires understanding each personality and securing non-artificial conditions in fine detail.
Says she did not want to make a 'concept for the sake of a concept', for the members or for herself.

Argues that an entertainment business only flourishes when producing and management run as one organism: music, visual concept, marketing and business must connect and move in unison; debating whether concept, music, members or marketing matters most is meaningless because they are tightly combined, and connecting the areas precisely to produce visible results is worth more than branding.

Says she chose five members with very different personalities and avoided overlapping positions or images so as not to create needless competition or stress; distinct individuals with their own strengths can show confidence and form stability, and she wanted an environment where they respect each other's individuality.
Hopes more diverse genres and forms of expression reach popular music and says she planned NewJeans with that in mind, as a welcome signal that moves the scene in a new direction.

Says she works meticulously but does not deliberately analyse the market: collecting and analysing signals already visible slows you down; she trusts unseen insight, focuses on the overall flow rather than fragments — reading the era's direction from universal public psychology, setting the big direction, and using fragments of trends only as details. Sometimes she ignores trends entirely, because when the goal and direction are clear and the work is well made, ignoring trends can be the more creative choice.

Denies that NewJeans' short tracks were made for short-form platforms: length follows each song's development; predictable verses or bridges are sometimes deleted for a refined flow and completeness; deciding length in advance would feel alien.

Says she founded the label to be its general producer and took the CEO role to make that independence complete: creation needs close coordination with management, not unlimited budgets; popular culture's success is measured in numbers because it is not pure art, so creation and management are equally important. Twenty years in the industry taught her mostly what not to do, especially from conflicts born of mutual misunderstanding between creative and management.

Rejects the framing that NewJeans was built on 'HYBE capital': label strategy after investment was the label's own discretion, she had other investment offers of similar size, and creative independence and non-interference would have been her first condition with any investor.

Says NewJeans' first-EP budget was planned from experience and market research and was not unusually large; relative to the output it was highly cost-efficient; a large budget does not guarantee good work, and she tries to balance creation against spending — which, together with the triple-title strategy, made unusually early revenue settlement to the members possible.

Says the decision to debut with three title tracks and several music videos surprised her staff and was possible only because she was both producer and CEO; producers must accept that popular art is not free of numbers, and being a creator rather than a non-creative manager let her design concepts and alternatives that generate numbers; accurate awareness of reality is what produces new plans.

Says that as a student she had no interest in idol culture and was critical, even pessimistic, about it — possibly why she entered it; at work she met many things she could not accept on logical grounds, and half-jokingly says she founded the label out of stubbornness to break long-standing conventions and prejudices.

Rejects readings that portray her as a successful idol fan or that her music videos project her own school days, noting she had no contact with idol culture in school; criticises attacks built on unverified hypotheses.

Describes structural contradictions of the idol industry — minors recruited and trained by company systems, fans wanting a stable company yet treating companies as adversaries by default — and says her relationship with NewJeans departs from the stereotyped company–artist relationship; she expects to prove that through work and results rather than argument.

Gives a concrete example of resisting industry habits: NewJeans albums did not include randomised photocards, because she wanted the content bought out of genuine feeling rather than a sales tactic; she wanted to test how far a straightforward approach — songs, choreography, content — could go, and for the same reason ran no paid YouTube promotion, since the less inflated the data, the more accurately you see reality and the bolder the next step can be.

Says becoming CEO did not change her work: she still makes things herself when they are new and hard to explain; she wants an unprecedented relationship with consumers; she founded ADOR to do interesting work, because 'fun' changes many things and is the essence of entertainment; early outputs she leads directly become precedents that guide staff.

Frames the idol industry as teamwork between adults and teenagers in which neither can succeed alone; NewJeans' members are learners, and treating trainees as 'artists' from debut day is unrealistic; she wanted no decoration or exaggeration to make them look impressive, preferring to show the joy of doing one's best whether or not one does well, and to reveal growth naturally — for the same reason she neither inflates nor hides her own role as planner.

Uses film as an analogy: audiences accept a director's intent in a film without calling actors puppets or saying the director is 'too visible'; she questions whose view the 'puppet' stereotype of idols really is, while saying she is not asking for idols to be seen as art.

Describes herself as a film and music obsessive from youth (citing the colour and narrative of Pedro Almodóvar and the unhurried plots and angles of Ozu Yasujirō) who listens across eras, nationalities and genres, and finds particular excitement in discovering hidden links between unrelated musicians through credits and tastes.

Says the world is full of great music and that music matters for everyday quality of life, and that she wants to deliver the experiences that excited her to the public in as many varied and enjoyable ways as possible.

Explains the winter release after the debut EP as a return gift: a warm lead song, a holiday pop-up, a commitment to donate part of sales, and a package conceived like a Christmas present (a planned children's-hospital visit was cancelled by COVID).

Says ADOR was founded to make the music and business she aims for, run differently from existing industry systems, from a desire to propose music and a vision absent from the mainstream; since she is not a songwriter she has no copyright stake, which frees her choices about song structure and selection; ADOR's music would be boundary-free in style, so working with people who understand her taste mattered more than routine organisational systems.

Says the condition she most strongly sought when launching ADOR inside HYBE was a firm guarantee of no interference in creative and operational autonomy, and that HYBE had no connection to ADOR's production.

Describes her music process: ADOR does not rely on a single composer; she collects and decides the music herself — NewJeans' first EP track list was assembled from a demo library she had collected before the group existed — and she refines details (mixing, mastering, vocal direction) to her intended direction in discussion with a long-time producer partner rather than the songwriters.

Names melody development and singing style as her key production criteria, and describes a strong aversion to typical K-pop conventions — obligatory high notes, abruptly inserted raps, uniform vocal delivery — while respecting those who like them; she took charge of the whole production in order to control such details and release work without them.

Argues that 'composition' is an ambiguous concept: beat-makers and top-liners contribute differently from song to song, so no single person makes a song, and the planner who coordinates the whole process carries more weight; the same composer's work sounds different under a different final decision-maker, so saying she 'picked' songs is both right and wrong.

Calls herself someone who wants to break formulas, specifically the K-pop 'success formula' others assert; wants a creative environment without prejudice and a market with more diverse ideas, noting the implication that this came from a former art director with no interest in idols.

Warns against reverse-engineering success from outcomes: every analysis is bounded by limited experience, titles mean different things across industries, and analysing something new by fitting it into old frames is itself outdated — the frame has to change for thinking to change. Her own tentative explanation of NewJeans' success: attractive beats and melodies plus vocals with every burdensome element removed, pleasant anywhere and anytime — a deliberate return to basics.

States strong antipathy to K-pop 'worldview' (lore) systems: NewJeans has no worldview in that sense, though she welcomes people who name its consistent message a worldview; she values curiosity and unexpected fun, and each release will voice the same context in a different way.

Points out a contradiction in welcoming both autonomous, self-directed idols and character-like constructed worldviews; argues popularity emerges from many interacting causes and cannot be attributed to lore, so there was no reason to cling to it; NewJeans would instead respond nimbly with the topic each moment calls for, as when a song was released as a reply to the debut album's reception.

Explains the 'deer in the snowfield' image for the Ditto video: hearing the demo's humming intro, she pictured a deer suddenly appearing in an empty snowfield and people encountering it — like NewJeans appearing in the world; the most beautiful thing is free in open space, and the onlookers' innocent wish to possess it can end up controlling it and halving its charm; she wanted to say that they shine more when left free, and to turn misunderstandings from the debut into reconciliation through a gift-like winter album.

Explains choosing director Shin Woo-seok for a release she wanted to look completely different from the debut: someone who had never made a K-pop video, without illusions about entertainment and working without boundaries; his first question was about NewJeans' long-term plan, which reassured her. She deliberately did not interfere, cast herself as an 'assistant director' supplying wardrobe and shooting conditions, and briefed purpose, industry realities, long-term direction and what the record should convey — explaining only the reason behind an impression (such as the deer), not a look and feel, so as not to damage his ideas.

Says choreography can be shown attractively in dance videos, so she produced several of those, while official music videos should carry larger meaning and a different value; she wants to show that some values matter more than view counts — a matter of conscience because she works with young members.

Describes her leadership: before working with any staff she explains the ultimate direction and purpose and then the plan in fairly concrete terms, because her blueprint is clear; with the members too she first explains what she is ultimately trying to do and say and why it matters, which she considers more important than explaining detailed concepts or stories; her role is to inspire, draw out and steer.

Says she asked from before the group's formation for non-typical freestyle choreography rather than idol-style precision group dancing; she cannot set specific moves, only explain the feel and direction, so when one first draft missed she re-explained and requested a full revision, which then succeeded; later routines were approved at once — capable people do well once direction is set and they are encouraged.

Says she built her own label partly to work with a settled mind, choosing across music, video and management people who share the direction; the prerequisite is that her own vision is sound enough to say 'follow me'. Micromanagement is neither good nor bad in itself — detailed alignment often requires it and it takes skill because the other person's feelings matter; there is no fixed answer in leading, so she adapts to each person and situation.

Explains why she rarely gives interviews: her work involves complex, context-dependent ideas that length-limited interviews distort, and the same words are understood differently by different readers; yet silence also breeds misunderstanding.

Says she does not use the word 'worldview' herself: when she conceives a direction a fitting narrative comes naturally, and she prefers natural flow and foreshadowing that reflect the subject's real self over artificially constructed settings (though settings are sometimes needed); she prefers throwing out a topic to fixing an ending, which leaves later developments far more autonomy.

Says titles stopped mattering to her long ago: when someone voluntarily works beyond a given role in pursuit of a clear goal, the role expands naturally and a single title becomes an obstacle; role expansion grows from doing the basic job well and cannot be forced.

Says she never limited her work to the visual: what counts is achieving the intended result and doing 'work with a soul'. Visual design alone is a small idea, though still central for contemporaneity and visibility; for visuals to become a real strength they require understanding of the non-visual areas and an intelligent fusion with them, and only new attempts built on expanding and combining business models can open new horizons of visual culture.

Says that to realise her big picture fully she needed the music she wants as the foundation, continuing into her own choices of casting, training, design and business — the clearer the blueprint, the more a label of her own becomes necessary.

Asked what the core of her sensibility is, says outsiders see only part of her work (most cite one f(x) album), but a thread runs through it: a staff member once said everyone in her photographs looks as if they have a story ('사연'); she wants her work to convey each individual's own, unpredictable story.

Describes the dilemma of working inside a stabilised industry: systems with their own protocols bring efficiency, stability, capital and an ecosystem, but dependence on systems drifts toward loss of individuality; she wanted to break the system while also preserving it, which required balance — and balance cannot be achieved by a strategy for one part of an organisation, only by an overall strategy, which is what led her to found a label.
Says that even when reality turns away from it, the minimum effort to protect the essence never betrays you, and that effort itself is a kind of energy.

Says she received many commercial offers (advertising, broadcasting, publishing) during her SM years and accepted none, and kept no social media, as an expression of her stance of not trading on fame; she opened Instagram and appeared on TV only at the end of 2021 because being invisible made her easier to misrepresent.

Doubts that today's culture of constant 'communication' is what was hoped for: real communication requires understanding the other side and takes deliberate effort, which is why she wants genuine communication with consumers on the business side — misunderstanding of carefully made work is painful.

Says a director bears inconsistent standards (personal blame for bad reviews, 'did she do it alone?' for good ones) and accepts that the person with overall responsibility receives both praise and criticism on everyone's behalf; what she objects to is groundless rumour and the flattening of complex, layered situations into one-line verdicts.

Explains her SM-era approach as a deliberate counter-position: affection expressed in a fixed, identical way quickly loses interest, and idol production and consumption showed that typicality; her directing started from the opposite of the established first-generation SM style, so it read as heterogeneous and provoked curiosity — a reaction she anticipated and calculated for.

Says unexpected work from a large organisation is welcome, and that she pursued it because it was necessary for the company's future rather than for visual polish; at the time there was no recognition of the importance of visuals, hence no budget or time for it, and it took a long time to establish it as a key strategy — over about ten years SM's approach to visual realisation was reorganised around her method, so she left without regret.
Argues that work efficiency comes from a person's own level of goal-consciousness, which cannot be implanted or formulated by others; efficiency injected from outside has limits.

Questions the premise that 'everyone' tries to escape stereotypes: many people actually want stability while professing to want newness. New things are necessarily unfamiliar and are often criticised before being examined, yet new is not automatically good: 'newness for newness's sake' — inertia wearing the mask of newness — must be distinguished; the focus should be on why newness is wanted, the underlying essence. Since newness is relative to each viewer, satisfying everyone with novelty is nearly impossible; her effort is to keep challenging toward newness while recalling the essence.

Defines the problem ADOR exists to solve as leaving the industry's routinised patterns and courageously creating alternative paths; says HYBE's leadership accepted that her approach differed from the chairman's and that coexisting different possibilities inside an organisation raise the probability of success, whereas mature industries tend to stagnate in stable methods.

Says she became CEO in order to exist as a creator: the roles are very different but deeply connected — commercial creative work that cannot be converted into capital loses vitality, businesses alien to their creative product rarely succeed, and ignoring that creation and capital are inseparable in commercial work tangles everything; she is not interested in the CEO title itself.
Says she prefers maximum closeness with fans rather than strategically managed distance; she has never intended 'push and pull' and prefers honesty and kindness in the work she leads.

Gives the group's timeline: auditions in September 2019, casting completed by the end of 2019, about two years of training from early 2020, initially a joint project planned for 2021 and delayed by COVID; the 2022 Q3 launch was chosen by weighing the burden of a rushed debut on young members against fans' waiting and market timing.

Says entertainment exists to entertain, not to break records or rank; she wants a situation where everyone does their best joyfully, since best effort grows out of enjoyment and itself needs practice — so the team aims at 'enjoying' rather than 'mastery', because the energy of people who truly enjoy makes the audience dance too.

Says investment in K-pop has grown sharply but supply and consumption have not developed in proportion; the change she most wants is a greater capacity to accept change, since similar content is mass-produced and consumed along fixed patterns; those who try can still find slightly different concepts, but no one can force a challenge that risks starvation — supply needs consumption — so both producers' and consumers' attitudes must improve; in cultural industries, diversity cannot exist without a prior willingness to accept newness.

Says she dislikes effort spent on looking good and is not fooled by it; kindness performed for show lacks spontaneity, becomes a chore and cannot last, so inner sincerity matters — especially in work aimed at the public.

Says casting and training are usually treated as separate from production, but she considers them essential to creative quality; as a creative director at SM she could not intervene in training, which was a reason to launch a label covering the whole process. When she took over the project in September 2021 her first steps were health and living-condition checks and the state of the dorm and practice rooms; she frames trainee life as a small school and asks staff to act as teachers.

Describes lyric-writing sessions for trainees as a literature and composition class: she explains the album concept and each song's direction, members share related experiences, and some of their writing is used in lyrics as a learning step; immature but brave, honest expression is valuable, and talent should be observed over time before being judged.

Describes the structural cost of changing an organisation from within: an individual must persuade company, colleagues and consumers; once achieved, the hard-won result is quickly taken for granted while it becomes a new system that lifts the company; in her experience credit flowed to the company and fault to the individual, which contributed to her leaving SM.

Says she did not leave SM for money and had not arranged a next job; despite outside perception of her as the embodiment of SM, she felt a distance from the company; she distinguishes loyalty to her work and loyalty between people (which she values) from unconditional loyalty to an organisation (which she does not have).

Says she disliked the strange distance between producers and consumers: gathering consumers' opinions is the basis of her work, which is impossible if the relationship is distant; she now wants to approach them sincerely first.

Anticipates the trap of expectation anchored on one past success: work similar to it will be called self-copying, work very different from it will disappoint; she treats this as a high-risk situation requiring care, and says that as a company operator her decisions will prioritise 'minimum conscience' even when profit pressures create dilemmas.

Says her SM work was never limited to art direction: she gave opinions on song selection and direction, renamed albums, once prompted an unprecedented staff vote that changed a title track, and planned a 2013 compilation album with 10 Corso Como made with various DJs.

Says she sought full authority for her label because all areas of production interlock; nobody knows what will be popular until it is released, so it is better to do what one genuinely wants; image-makers are acutely affected by music, which is why she made trailers that emphasise a song's mood (e.g. SHINee's 'Odd – View' series); good images are maximised by good music — not because music matters most but because the pleasure peaks when all areas harmonise, which is also why business matters.

Says she wrote the initial plan and presentation scenario for 'HYBE: New Brand Presentation' (2021), an unprecedented format that worried people until it was finished, and prepared it with two named colleagues; the most rewarding reaction was outsiders asking why they were enjoying another company's corporate briefing, since such briefings are usually boring; she describes a basic desire to surprise people in an enjoyable way.

Credits a long-time colleague (director Kim Ye-min) with substantial contributions, and says the EXO 'Pathcode' promotion was run by a three-person task force including the two of them, self-initiated as strategically necessary like the f(x) art film; she argues that headcount and quality are not proportional — accurate understanding and intense concentration within the time available matter more.

Says the industry needs people who think differently in the mainstream; she is frustrated by claims that 'this style works' or 'this is the answer' — if such formulas existed everyone would succeed; she naturally projects her taste, wants to introduce what she likes, and always weighs its intersection with popular culture; goodness cannot be reduced to one style, and not being a music producer frees her to choose across styles; good things stay good over time.
Says the HYBE headquarters design focused on making a space where people want to stay, out of a wish that employees be happy at work.

Describes music as governing the mood of a space and recalling moments; in youth, digging for music was a skill (taping songs from the radio); recalls being moved by hearing instruments separately yet in extraordinary harmony in a bossa-nova recording; shares a 12-track reference list spanning 1964–2017 and several countries (Brazilian, Italian, Japanese, French, Korean, American), while warning that her personal taste should not be read as a preview of her group's music — taste and business are different matters.

On judging success: criteria differ by person; self-satisfaction comes first but work without empathy risks becoming mere self-indulgence, and popularity driven by fame regardless of the work's density can be an illusion; so the measure of success ends up in rigorous self-scrutiny, finding one's own way between self-satisfaction and self-criticism.

Describes her drive as short-term goals plus curiosity: reaching a goal changes the conditions and produces the next goal; she imagines how things will change rather than wishing; she distinguishes this, and a sense of responsibility, from 'loving work' — she has loyalty to her work rather than reverence for it.

Design press (2013) describes her as SM's head of visual direction covering album design, stage costume and now music videos, a scope that grew as feedback on her work accumulated; when she joined, entertainment design was 'a wasteland'. She is quoted comparing the work to making an advertisement.

Girls' Generation's 4th album 'I Got a Boy' was released as ten packages (one group version plus nine member photobook versions) — described as turning the album itself into merchandise — with a collaboration with a Korean street-wear label for stage costumes and merchandise (including a 'boys' version for male fans), per-member Hangul-initial logos, and a merchandise pop-up café.
projects: Girls' Generation I Got a Boy

claim: The magazine describes SHINee's concept as a 'free boy' with non-mainstream sensibility, departing from the established SM image, with her leading its look and feel; f(x) as 'an unknowable girl', with album covers using only illustration and no face photos — unusual enough for an idol album to be described as shocking.

EXO's logo was built from basic geometric shapes expressing the group's 'exoplanet' origin story, designed to be applied to accessories, merchandise and stage costumes and to persist across albums; the two sub-units received black and white versions of the package.

Says she became involved in stage costume and overall concept from Girls' Generation's 'Gee' and from SHINee's and f(x)'s debuts, and oversees albums, videos and promotion packages; for a recent SHINee video she recommended a director with a new way of working to tie it to the graphic elements and proposed new graphic methods beyond costume meetings; the scope came from doing assigned work steadily while constantly proposing new ideas that produced good results.

Says that before there was a director responsible for visuals everything was disjointed: great music fails with mismatched costumes and vice versa; even when commissioning outside designers, the key is to set a precise concept, find the person best able to realise it, and connect every image organically.

Defines the entertainment designer's job as planning and managing what musicians cannot attend to beyond the music — visual marketing that shows their appeal — necessary because the era is saturated with images; the most important thing is the musician's identity, and since public response depends on how that appeal is expressed, everything must interlock like gears.

Argues that a logo or character is not right for every act: for a group that transforms its image each release, a fixed logo constrains the graphics and cannot carry contrasting concepts (a strong uniformed look one time, a girlish one the next); EXO instead has a logo from basic shapes carrying the group's philosophy and values, flexible in use — the method is chosen per act, not applied uniformly.

Says she worries that teenagers who enjoy pop music experience only a narrow culture and wanted to show them other things; the work must be neither too difficult nor — which she dislikes even more — too easy and light, but satisfy both at once; fans decoding hidden metaphors and symbols was part of the pleasure.

Explains teaser sequencing: for every teaser photo she calculates why it is released at that moment, its order, and the small part of feeling it should draw from the audience; for f(x) she wanted to keep throwing the album's metaphors without ever letting the audience's anticipation drop, so immersion and understanding rise together.

Says she photographed the 'Red Light' teasers and album herself: it let her release thirteen teasers a day because she could judge coverage while shooting, and the concept had many parts that could not easily be explained to others; album work sits closest to fine art within commercial art, which makes the art director's role distinctive.

Explains 'Red Light' as expanding the song's 'warning' by juxtaposing or paralleling opposed codes (taboo and longing, utopia and dystopia, reality and ideal) — the half-made-up face expresses this; teasers ran from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., thirteen in total, numbers people quietly treat as taboo; the aim was that viewers, stimulated by images and talking about them, would 'hear' the music with eyes and mouth as well as ears.

Asked whether such attempts are risky for an idol group needing mass appeal, says the real risk is the boredom of uniformity; nobody wants to be consumed like a doll, and artists want their work to mean something — hence trying something minor in the most major place. Minor is not good or bad in itself; minor things are harder to accept, but difficult things make people think, and she likes making things that make people think.

Says she wanted to extract surreal images from real, existing places (an idol placed still in an industrial neighbourhood) because fear lives inside reality and reality and ideal are closer than they seem; the release used two photo tones and two album designs, some grotesque, some unrealistically beautiful; the cover shot of members fleeing a flower field was in fact them running from insects — an unintended moment she captured because it delivered the natural direction she wanted.

Describes f(x)'s releases as an unfolding story: the first single invited outsiders into a mysterious private space (no need to show everything at first), the first album fixed the identity, a later album revealed fragile, twisted instincts, and 'Pink Tape' told of secret love and self-awareness — continuity across releases without a fixed lore.

Explains the bear on the 'Electric Shock' cover: an animal that can kill becomes, with a small change of expression, the teddy bear children sleep with; she wanted the 'shock' to read not simply as love but as the ironic, universal fact that a shock trivial to one person can be terror to another.

Says an art director must basically be a storyteller: she constantly imagines scenarios unprompted, and when a song arrives she chooses among stored ideas the story that would be interesting to tell with that music.

Explains her recurring boy/girl imagery by the members' youth — it is natural to wear clothes that fit one's body — and by a professed fondness for incomplete, immature beings and the universal longing for the purest moment.

On EXO's 'Growl' street shoot: the intended feeling was the thrill of running into someone you like in your own neighbourhood, a momentary fantasy inside the ordinary; she asked the members to drop self-conscious expressions and be indifferent, so the images feel outside time and place.

Explains why she began photographing albums herself: partly because her concept was hard to transmit to another photographer, but more because the longer she designs the more she subtracts — like architects drifting toward minimalism — wanting only the essence; sometimes doing nothing is the best design, so she began seeking a single image that is complete on its own, approaching photography as graphic design in the broad sense rather than wanting to be a photographer.

Says her training came from directing shoots (situations, poses, styling changes, angles, tone, even the on-set music); she learned only the basic camera controls, relying on an understanding of light from drawing, because the goal of an album-cover photo is not a technically perfect portrait but the expression of a subtle emotion; she prefers finding a method from not-knowing over following others, and above all dislikes obvious images.

For a member's first solo album she chose to express him as he is, without additions, avoiding excessive settings in favour of situations that allow delicate emotion, adding to the subject's own intensity an image that lets each viewer dream their own version.

Says joining a mainstream idol company was a deliberate calculation: because her own taste (world music) was different, she expected to be effective there — provided the company accepted her ideas — and that unexpected combinations are more interesting.

Says her remit began to widen when, though not yet in overall charge, she made specific proposals for Girls' Generation's debut: rather than decorating singers prettily, which bored her, she proposed a healthy, refreshing image that would stand out in a harsh entertainment world and appeal to men and women alike; the cover took its motif from 'Little Women' (distinct sisters in harmony). She did not labour over storytelling: when what you want to show is clear, the story follows and can be left to viewers' imagination — which she calls a real concept.
projects: Girls' Generation debut (Into the New World)

claim: Says she preferred to give SHINee and f(x) an identity from formation rather than inject fragmentary images, explaining the intended direction at length early on; the music industry must always think about the 'next generation', which means looking not for something better or grander but for something different from what came before.

Says she generally does not favour a single symbol or logo-work for albums, but judged EXO needed one: its premise (superpowered beings from an unknown planet) was hard to make credible, so a symbol embodying the concept would organise the story and lend persuasiveness; applying the symbol in varied ways rather than repeating it identically would make the story grow over time.

Criticises branding-through-design that becomes over-systematised: design dances on the border between art and business, and the answer lies between meticulousness and looseness; a piece with no gaps is less attractive, so she always leaves breathing room; good branding reflects philosophy and purpose naturally, so she takes a somewhat abstract approach instead of a fixed algorithm — each piece varied, but each with sufficient reason.

On design awards: with records, music comes first and design second, so competitive awards feel odd; record design is unique in that memories of listening transform even crude covers (she recalls a soundtrack cover she disliked becoming precious through the music); she wanted to start an interesting movement and draw attention to design in the Korean music industry rather than make masterpieces — there is no royal road in record design.

Argues that falling album sales did not reduce the importance of images: concepts of consumption and collecting changed and mixed analog and digital, while image consumption and involvement grew; the role of an image imprinted in someone's mind is the same in any format.

Says the Pink Tape art film led to her taking on music-video production: from late 2014 a new team she led was created alongside SM's existing video team, with artists split between teams; in 2015 she made EXO, Red Velvet and SHINee videos, while other directors handled the visuals of acts she was not involved with; the benefit was tighter links between video and album art and clearer follow-through on intent.

Says she works with an imagined consumer who can select and discern good things; 'good' exists before personal preference but cannot be objectively defined, so it is found by people who enjoy selecting according to their own situation and taste.

Says she prefers to explain only an outline of her metaphors and symbols rather than fix their meaning; different readings are the viewer's right and cannot be forced; she prioritises work that is fundamentally convincing regardless of taste, with taste judgments coming after.

Says her taste inevitably enters the work (once suppressed, now released); she does not worship mass appeal but treats it as important in her position, noting her mass hits too; building a portfolio widened by diverse attempts benefits everyone and expands the market, whereas multiplying similar entities in a limited market is foolish; strategy is needed as paradigms change, but strategy is only strategy — the priority is always the essence, making 'good things' rather than chasing someone's taste.

Says she starts every project bolder than she intends, because things inevitably get trimmed during production — and tells video directors never to lower their own ambition — then manages intensity toward the end so it does not overreach; she judges by her own standard, asking others mainly to check first reactions, since an uninformed first reaction is the most honest.
Names the non-negotiable as the intended purpose: if the original intent is damaged during production, she goes back to the start.

Says even her boldest projects involved realistic compromises (for example, an album with no photos at all is hard to get approved); since no commercial work is free of constraints, she tries to use the given situation to 200 percent.

Describes references as emotions from good films and music that accumulate as working energy rather than being applied directly: she cites a film's opening sequence for the harmony of still images and music, asked a video team to study the balance between an intimate camera angle and music in another film's opening — explicitly not to copy any scene — and, when a photographed model suggested a film character, gave no reference photo or explanation, because the model need not know; she works from her own interpreted, intertwined atmosphere, which is how taste enters the work.

Describes a magazine shoot she was invited to direct after a publication asked who had photographed the f(x) teasers: she built a dramatic sequence around an obscure Italian song found while digging, inserting it in a short film, because the unexpected harmony of an odd combination is uniquely attractive.
Says groups need not all be made the same way; each should have its own method — and declines to explain a new group's identity in advance so the audience will look for it themselves.

Chooses collaborators by taste and individuality and by how their taste could affect the project; is curious about others' thinking and wants to gather its essence; defines the creative director's role as collecting and coordinating new ideas into a result nobody could have imagined, thinking about how to use someone's discretion rather than waiting for a perfect fit; persuasion starts with making work that convinces, by stressing the purpose and justification.

Describes her early work at SM as cultivating a wasteland and the transitional period of building systems as combative; as her work developed, the industry moved with it; she values self-satisfaction over praise and keeps seeing what could be fixed in past work.

Says that on joining Big Hit she was given three tasks — complete the company rebranding, launch a girl group, and launch a label of her own — and that she wanted the label to plan records including the music, using twenty years of insight to throw interesting questions into the industry.

Defines the rebranding as rebuilding the brand identity and brand system and extending it into the new headquarters; she treated the move not as a relocation but as a main axis of the brand system because space creates attitude — good branding contains the process of forming the attitude you want — and wanted to show how a graphic philosophy continues into space.

Says branding confined to graphics always bored her and she wanted to extend graphic value into 2D→3D→4D; since space is replaced on long cycles it must be done right the first time; she wanted an office unlike any other, not newness for its own sake but to give employees real welfare in the form of space — comparable to her wish to surprise people with albums.

Describes doing unprecedented work as colliding with inertia and old practice; practices exist for reasons and cannot simply be dismissed, but the larger the organisation the more inertial thinking runs, and people lose the essence by rushing to process tasks instead of attending to results and context; 'newness' is invisible to some, so persuading is hard; everyone agrees inertia is bad yet fails to recognise it in their own choices — the options are to fight it laboriously or to prove the essence with good results.

Says she worked weekly with the architects as one team for about eighteen months from concept to inspection, studying details as problems arose — e.g. testing light samples for colour rendering and eye fatigue — because a space's atmosphere depends heavily on light and sound.
Redefines working 'smart' not as compressed, organised, systematic process but as finding one's own process that reaches the essence most faithfully and fastest.

Names 'no coercion' as the governing idea for the office: research showed companies imposing playful interiors (colourful furniture, childlike amenities) in the name of welfare, an implicit compulsion to relax; rest is a form of consideration that no one can force, and good things are easily imposed precisely because they are good — so the skill is to guide naturally without imposing.

Describes the office as a gathering of experts that requires respect, and names a 19th-floor birch garden 'COMB' — the row of birches suggested a comb, and the name expresses combing tangled thoughts back to their natural state; birch was chosen because few species survive in a concrete building and slender trees keep a narrow space from feeling cramped.

Says she recognises that her position as client lets her change the flow of work, while her role as a maker also matters, and that acknowledging different people's capacities and responsibilities is the precondition for unprecedented results.

Says eighteen years of artist branding made corporate branding feel continuous with it; explains branding as like tidying — choosing, arranging and using things that suit your space so as to imprint an image — since every way of arranging produces an impression whether intended or not; artist images form from why content is made, chosen and promoted, so good branding does not end at a BI or a building but must be maintained, repaired and used sustainably.

Says branding induces attitudes whose accumulation forms the brand; 'newness' fades with time like a mirage, so the point of the headquarters was not to create a new face or space but to lay the foundation for the attitude that suits the company.

Says she likes the 'hidden real': what is real cannot be grasped from the surface; this is not withholding as a game — people should be able to take the work intuitively without knowing, and if they later realise the intent, so much the better, and wrong readings are fine; feelings one discovers oneself differ greatly from feelings produced by injected information, and the moment of self-discovered 'this is good' becomes an unforgettable memory; she says all her past work was made this way.

Says she was involved down to base materials, chairs and lights, ignoring warnings that 'nobody works this way', because she wanted to give roughly a thousand employees only things she had tried and found good.

Says the widening scope of her work felt natural rather than burdensome because everything is connected — a good music video requires good music first, so she always gave opinions on the music, and job boundaries dissolved; years into SM she told a friend she had not left because her 'homework' was not finished.
Adds that the K-pop scene did not feel interesting to her at the time, and that a new attempt only becomes meaningful at the right moment — which is why she judged that moment to be an opportunity.

Describes the producer role as overseeing every process of making a record, from the music onward, and her own path as graphic designer → art director → creative director → producer, the last growing out of a long interest in music and a wish, formed on the job, to make records carrying her intent.

Explains releasing NewJeans' music videos first instead of the usual teaser → video → audio sequence: she asked what she would find fun as a member of the public; did not want to keep those anticipating the group waiting; and wanted to convert peak attention into listening — since good music goes unheard without promotion and people will watch at least once when attention is highest, she used that first view to deliver three title songs.

Denies targeting 'retro': trends are like a Möbius strip — things she liked as a child are now fashionable with teenagers — so the aim was to make good things that she and the members like and would want to own, with the cyclical nature of trends included only as one element of fun.

Says experience taught her that a change you create returns like a wave in an unpredictable shape and time, so rather than fearing waves she tries to ride them with quick responsiveness while showing what was prepared step by step.

Says she expected the debut to be liked — not as confidence of commercial victory but because she had prepared music she believed in — and held both anxiety that confident work might be rejected and eagerness to show it.

Says she collected demos herself from around 2019, when she first conceived the team and before it had a name — including a single to be released in January 2023 — choosing songs in her own preferred style that friends would put in their playlists; releasing the debut felt like publishing her personal playlist.

Says she wanted a team making music of a feeling she had long imagined, because of doubts and disagreements accumulated over a long idol-industry career; her planning and execution differ from established ones, so she had to persuade often but proceeded regardless; her interest was music from the start, and a different viewpoint and approach became strengths once hurdles were cleared.

Defines her idea of a sophisticated team as grounded in naturalness, which cannot be turned into a concept, taught or forced; people of that age are most attractive as they are, so she prioritised empathy over instruction, built an environment where members could be honest — honesty itself being an asset — and valued mutual trust, aiming to show them as unfiltered as possible.

Says new challenges bring anxiety and anxiety makes people unnatural, so trust among collaborators comes first; problems differ with each person's character, so there is no single fix; she explained first, honestly, why she does the work and wanted the members to find their own reasons — which she considers more important than dance or vocal training.
Says a first album cannot explain everything and that the intended direction will be conveyed gradually through the discography.
Explains naming the fandom 'Bunnies' before debut: she considers fans genuine friends, so they are given the same name as the members' rabbit image — the same species, best friends.

Says Apple's first proposal was a choreography video showcasing a camera feature; she counter-proposed shooting the main music video on the phone so that the act of filming with it carried meaning, confident this would be better for the brand too — an unprecedented arrangement Apple accepted.

Explains matching the phone-shot video to the fast, hard-hitting track rather than a flash-mob song or a mood piece, because camera movement would show best there; the choreography was planned from the outset to be filmed on the phone.

Says she did not want merely to highlight a feature: the phone's meaning in modern life is complex; the track is cheerful yet sorrowful, like the video's story and like life — bright on the surface, different inside — and she likes work that conveys such a three-dimensional view to widen how it can be appreciated.

Explains making separate videos for many songs out of affection for each: images maximise the range of appreciation, so a video should make people want to replay the song while also raising appreciation of the song without the video; videos without the musicians on screen are not new — what matters is the message; in the mood-driven video, the detached observer characters are effectively the protagonists, inviting reflection on what a protagonist is.

Explains 'Super Shy': on first hearing she instinctively pictured many people in one space repeating the same moves; the repetitive beat, simple but rising structure and 'shy' theme suggested addictive repetition, so she asked the choreography director for easy moves anyone could follow, imagined as a flash mob; the EP was framed as symmetrical to the debut EP, like a lock and key — the first invited people into the group's world, this one sends the group out into the world.

Defines collaboration as a meeting of distinct ideas that must satisfy both sides and create synergy; rather than creating situations that require hard persuasion, she tries first to make something self-evidently convincing — the bunny logo morphing into the partner's logo needed no persuasion.

Says she dislikes formulas — a fun culture has none; teasers exist to raise curiosity but had become a mere custom, and with attention already high they were unnecessary; curiosity about never-seen content would create more buzz, and the goal was to turn that curiosity into actually listening, because the new concept was the music itself — unconventional for idol music and therefore needing time for the public to get used to it, which the music videos were designed to provide by inducing repeat listening.

Explains the debut's information withholding: members' names were not disclosed and each member was styled drastically differently in each video, deliberately confusing, so viewers would rewatch all four videos to work out who was who and search online — making fans keep 'studying'; for a rookie with no fan base, securing a fandom quickly was key, and she expected this to generate voluntary buzz.

Argues that people wrongly treat 'concept' as purely visual; with today's overflow of media and visual techniques nothing visual feels new, so focusing only on visualising is foolish; a good concept cannot be pinned to one factor — what makes you feel complex feelings yet draws you in is a truly good concept.

Says she wanted her own label solely for the music: having worked for over a decade where visual and musical departments were separated, she wanted to make albums of exactly the music she wanted, which required an environment free of outside intervention — independence was her only condition; not being a composer, ADOR's music would not be defined by one style.

Says she had felt tacitly forced to follow the formula for producing K-pop hits and, feeling rebellious, wanted to break it; she questioned whether 'public appeal' itself had been crammed into everyone by repetition, and found it disheartening that everyone aimed at similar styles to guarantee success.

Says she briefed the confirmed members on her direction and concept at her home, and that inside HYBE some called the concept 'plain' or lacking public appeal because it did not follow conventional idol 'grammar'; she proceeded because her vision was clear and she was confident in the music, and the scepticism made her want to release it sooner.

Says proposing something different can be scary but, once accepted, it writes new history; describes NewJeans as meant to be 'whimsical' — not quirky for its own sake but trying what K-pop should have done and had not — with the next release already planned before debut.

Says that when sequencing an album she wants every track to stand out; where the first EP gave its three title songs deliberately different impressions, the second EP did the opposite, making tracks one to six feel connected as one piece.

Says she asked the choreographer to build moves around filming on a phone, which she felt suited the group and its generation (young people use phones whenever they hang out), and suggested the members freely make up the end of the performance as if playing with friends, varying it each stage, so they could express themselves and viewers could feel real-time empathy.
Explains that she long avoided appearing on camera partly on purpose: if the producer steps forward too much, the artists who should be the protagonists can be overshadowed.
TV recap reports that in her late SM years she made as many as four or five music videos a month alongside album production.
Says she felt heavy pressure at debut because the members came with their own dreams, and that one cannot do this work without taking responsibility for those dreams.

Says she tells the members daily that it is fine to get things wrong as long as a joyful atmosphere comes through; money and success are good, but any work without joy is painful, so her hope is that the members become joyful people.
Members recount her repeated advice that work done with enjoyment is felt by the audience too ('you can't beat joy'), and that learning to genuinely enjoy took practice and preparation.

Says that at SM she was a producer who stayed out of the spotlight, and that in her early interviews she accepted only written (print) interviews, writing her own answers in her own voice and working only with outlets that would not rewrite them, because writing is how she restrains and controls what she says.

Describes her language: thought runs faster than speech, but in writing she uses very refined wording; she prefers a direct style in writing as in speech because indirection feels cowardly to her, and she strongly dislikes verbose, meandering prose — aiming to stay clear even when sentences run long.

Explains why she began appearing in media before NewJeans' launch: her role had expanded from visual direction to setting the direction of every area, and since people do not absorb new things like sponges — anything that goes against inertia triggers a rebound, positive or negative — she wanted to 'cushion' that rebound by giving context, so the public could understand that a planner of that character might produce such work; the point was not her personal image but the planner's intent and will.
Says that for ooak records she thinks that context-setting work is already done and she can go straight ahead.
Says her taste was essentially complete by about age nineteen, formed by the sheer volume of what she watched, read and heard as a child; afterwards she simply keeps taking things in as time allows.

Describes a childhood experience of traditional ink preparation as a bodily lesson in materials: the difference in density between hand-ground ink and bottled ink, how viscosity changes the brush stroke, the order and cleanliness of the scholar's desk — giving her an early sense of the difference between what is properly made and what is not.

Recalls that as a child she remembered films as visual shock rather than narrative — e.g. a spy film's title sequence as a huge graphic 'media wall', the costumes, backgrounds and interiors — reading films as visual text; she agrees the female characters were narratively flat, but says the visual language was a separate matter that she could absorb on its own.

Says that in her SM job interview she politely but bluntly critiqued the company's existing work — what was lacking in costumes and album jackets — and brought alternatives, also admitting she did not much like pop music; as an art student she had designed album covers (for acid-jazz and bossa-nova artists) as coursework.
Says that during a break from university she interned at an advertising agency, then a fashionable industry, where she spent time in the agency's small art-book library.

Says music lovers learn early to tell what is genuine regardless of genre; she loves all genres because each has its virtues and does not rank them, yet within every genre she picks out the things that match her own style — so her playlist becomes a genre of its own.

Explains her early motivation: high art requires deliberate effort to encounter, whereas popular music is with people constantly; making the visual art of popular music is therefore a beautiful kind of people's art — like Korean folk painting, which reached far more people than scholars' art; showing good artwork to teenagers and people in their twenties raises their quality of life and sensibility; she says she cannot work without a cause, and that to raise the level of popular culture the ordinary things young people see often must get better.

Says she never wanted to direct feature films because she would have too much to say to organise into one; she is good at depicting short fragments; she regards about two hours as the best length for concentrated, serious content that holds attention.
Names the films, music and books she encountered casually between about five and fifteen as the source of her inspiration — the nutrients she still draws on in her work.

Refuses to name a single favourite or 'best' film: each work has its own specialness and preciousness (which is why she drew a single flower, not a bouquet), so she can list loved works but not rank one above all; a third party may love a work even more than its maker.

Says that when she acts as director of her own content she attends to every scene, including the passing transitional ones, because for the scenes everyone remembers to land, the seemingly trivial 'bridge' moments around them are crucial; the films she chose to show are all ones with extraordinary bridge scenes.
Says she chose films that are not rare but that people do not know or would be unlikely to pick themselves.

Defends a clumsy, clichéd commercial film she loves: not every work can be a masterpiece, and the journey of a maker toward good work — including imperfect stops along the way — is meaningful; what moved her was the sincerity and purity visible in it and the leads' shining youth; she values 'tacky' period pop for the languid feeling it carries, because a world filled only with full and perfect things is boring — empty, clumsy charm gives people's lives breathing room.
Singles out an ending in which the story continues under the credits with the music as what completes a film, and as proof that the director and actors made it sincerely and enjoyed it.

Defines a 'first work' not as the chronologically first but as the first piece that precisely contains what one wanted to say; NewJeans was her first in that sense, yet she could not put everything into it because she followed a staged roadmap and paced it to how fast the public could digest new things; she is now preparing another 'first work' in a different territory, since her SM, NewJeans and current domains differ in scope rather than category.
