Says she has always watched things from a third-person, almost omniscient standpoint — asking how something was made and with what thought — rather than only being absorbed in it.

Distinguishes being calculating from strategic thinking: she describes herself as impulsive and instinctive but strategic, with strategy anchored in goodwill and a larger cause; she defines the cool thing ('멋') as having a cause and making the process toward it as clean as possible, not looking good in front of a camera.

Defines good direction partly as not being boring; she loves a slow director anyway for his characters, landscapes and 'vibe' and for drawing out thoughts people cannot easily say, which feel contemporary despite the period; she dislikes contrived styles, while granting that even a contrived film can have virtues, and says she loves momentary beauty.

Says that as someone in popular culture she dislikes the tedious and likes things that are fun yet special; her impulse is to pick good things that are little known or prejudged and hand them to people — like bringing a useful seed home — sharing what only she knows because it would be good if everyone knew; the collector's wish to keep things to oneself faded into joy in sharing.
Notes that when you retell something too vividly, listeners pre-imagine it and can be disappointed by the real thing — over-hyping sets up a gap between expectation and experience.

Says she likes things that are beautiful but dry, not beautiful but cloying; she cannot enjoy overly sentimental romantic comedies, though warm films that are not syrupy remain dear to her even with clichés.

Defines direction as the maker's intent driving the work, expressed through a grammar of one's own (framed structure, road movie, chronology); a movement like the Nouvelle Vague broke classical grammar so that a maker's stream of consciousness could be expressed.

Says she envied how Truffaut made a masterpiece by ignoring established method and expressing his own consciousness; notes that both the Nouvelle Vague and bossa nova mean 'new wave', and that bossa nova sophisticatedly absorbed popular elements into jazz; across music, film, art and culture she loves the transitional moment when something minor rises into the major.

Describes herself as a popular rather than a minor person who stands on the boundary, and says things rise from the minor to that boundary for a reason; her well-received work and NewJeans hit that point; she says people sense something is empty without knowing what, while she believes she knows — her intuition is that people will like something because it itches now and nobody is scratching it, and the time to scratch is when it itches most.

Describes her method with collaborators: she attends to almost every part herself and prefers small teams who understand her intent, yet she respects their methods and rarely touches their work — if she had to nag about everything she would do it herself. The industry thrives when diverse talents patchwork well, so the first rule is not to touch what a skilled person is skilled at, and the second is to guide them well — opening a path for their specialty to emerge without damaging it, which she sees as the director's role; the work inevitably becomes hers as director, so she must take care not to erode theirs. Her job is to lay the 'board' well — choosing the soil and feeding it — because beautiful things cannot take root in rotten ground.

Says such a team takes several rounds of working together and starts with checking whether the collaborator's path matches hers (someone only interested in quick money does not fit a long-term aim); for each project she prioritises sharing the purpose and attitude — with Movieland too, the first conversation was about why they wanted to do it, not which films; the best sign is when the other side understands without explanation.
Says precious things are hard to obtain and things obtained easily are tired of easily; new value only emerges after patient, persistent activity that slowly creates diversity.

Describes her current task as finishing the job she set herself when founding a label: to turn the business 'board' itself. Despite K-pop's growth, stagnant water rots and someone must open the channel; the industry is captured by illusions — talk of success spread by word of mouth rather than real numbers; revenue is easy to inflate, but operating and net profit — what is actually kept — determine whether everyone involved can sustain the business healthily; opening the flow creates breakthroughs and more for people to enjoy, which matters more to her than money itself.

Says that when looking for a breakthrough she dislikes changing only the surface: swapping a green shirt for a yellow one barely registers, whereas changing the whole look reveals a new person; likewise, when the public is bored, a business should not change the shirt colour but change the whole board.

Says diverse cultural experience in childhood matters because children have no prejudices; a book's imagined world can surpass any film adaptation; the many strange things she absorbed widened her thinking, and in any field — finance, mathematics, research — the most creative people tend to be culturally literate; creativity, the protruding human act, remains a fundamental virtue that AI cannot imitate.

Argues that algorithms make people chase only what they already chase, so in an era of infinite content someone has to spread the unexpected; and that the stronger online life becomes, the more offline experience gains power as a counter-reaction — hence the value of watching films together in a cinema.

Says the films she chose all have an extraordinary harmony of music and image — not strong narratives but a palpable 'air' or atmosphere; one of them is almost entirely bridge scenes with no climax, its driving shots seen from a passenger's view homaged by countless later films.

Says that as a former designer, art director and creative director she feels a responsibility, aesthetically and in direction, to pick works with meaningful points rather than pretentious art films; she deliberately did not rewatch them before the talks so as to experience them again together with the audience, since discussing them from old memory would be insincere.

Describes the 'power of taste': if you gather what you genuinely like without forcing it, the artists turn out to be connected — one musician's influences, sessions or film scores lead to others you already loved — like a shared taste DNA.
Observes that supporters commonly begin by saying they never liked idols or popular culture before — which she reads as the work drawing people from outside the category into a new experience.

Says expectation is not a burden but excitement; the only tension she feels is anticipation just before a release, because she knows the cue sheet — she deliberately designs where the climaxes fall in set lists, track lists and cue sheets (for example a surprise number at a stadium fan meeting) — and the peak pleasure is the moment just before a reveal, such as the minute before the debut video went live.

Says her energy comes from creation itself: her staff are the first audience — if their faces light up when she shares the plan, it works; she then develops it and briefs directors, whose excitement is a second signal; each is given a clear role, and the shared thrill bonds the team; collaborators do not want to show her something embarrassing and she must not give a weak direction, so they push each other upward.

Says she feels little creative anguish because she never starts vaguely: she finds ideation by aimlessly spreading out references ('what should we do?') frustrating, and instead starts from purpose — why this work, why make this group; with NewJeans she had music and images she wanted to show, and wanted to prove that a market everyone called saturated still had a gap. The root is wanting to share good things so they are felt precisely as good — like ordering courses in a meal so the pairing works.

Says the sequence and environment of encounter matter: like a surprise whose impact depends on the path to the reveal, NewJeans was kept under strict secrecy so no prejudice formed, so people would meet everything at once; the pre-debut billboard showing only her name and 'girl group' in a deliberately rough default typeface was meant to stand out among glossy luxury billboards — 'let's make it really crappy' — provoking passers-by to ask what it was.
Says she thinks of the public as her friends or classmates — people she wants to surprise and to give good things to.

Says she picked one film above all for its opening sequence: only a flowering tree, the sky and a song, no people — yet it seemed to tell the whole film's content, provoking curiosity while also setting everything in order.

Says that although she likes clear-cut answers in temperament, her taste always prefers blank space, ambiguity and 'holes'; even clumsy direction has an aesthetic, because young performers' real youth produces an aura no director could stage — an unintended moment caught on camera.

Criticises the present in which everyone tries too hard to be cool: work is too well-made, makers know style so well that they avoid any clumsiness, and young creators — filmmakers and graphic designers alike — are dense, high-density and professional from the start; she prefers the clumsiness of early work, as in children's drawings.

Describes how her period tastes changed: her ideal was the late 1960s–early 1970s for its precision and sophistication; when young she found the 1980s tacky and the late 1990s–early 2000s awkwardly pretending to be sophisticated, and wanted to change that aesthetic; only later did she come to appreciate 1980s maximalism and see that every era had its moment of aesthetic triumph.

Says she included a clumsy commercial film to show that beauty can be found in awkwardness — the raw, unrefined beauty of mass-produced local American culture that nonetheless came out of a refined system — an imbalance she wanted to share precisely because people would never pick it themselves.

Says she does not much like idol-style knife-sharp synchronised dancing because it is too mechanical; some find catharsis in mass-game precision, but by temperament she finds charm in the empty and the slightly awkward rather than in mechanical beauty.

Says she used to dislike the phrase 'repaying you with good work' as hypocritical, since makers work for themselves; but after hearing countless people say the group's music gave them strength while ill, she now feels she must not disappoint — her stance shifted from showing something fun to an unspecified public toward wanting to satisfy people more kindly.

Says surprise without meaning is less fun; work feels worth doing when it makes money, grows the industry and creates new people and opportunities — when she can feel it contributes something to the world.

Distinguishes the artisan path from the 'board-maker' path: she deeply respects artisans and chose not to remain one, because craft alone could not resolve her frustration; the two must coexist — artisans need someone who designs the board so they can make a living, and she finds her fun there; she is impatient for feedback, loves surprising people, and enjoys proving ability on small budgets ('this little money, this much result') like a game.

Explains why sharing her taste publicly is part of the work: people who encounter an unfamiliar aesthetic widen their range, as a picky child given a well-cooked vegetable learns to eat it; understanding the maker's context deepens enjoyment of later work; and she believes we are in an era when taste is becoming more refined and dense, with people spending on finer sensory detail.
Says cinemas that show only blockbusters are boring; small, specific experiences — screening a loved film for others — create more happiness than conspicuous luxury.
Admires a director who has an unmistakable fixed style yet such free imagination within it that development, direction and art are always unexpected, with hardly a disappointing film across a career.

Says the films she chose look like mood pieces on the surface but are 'strong' inside — one a story of resistance against legacy systems wrapped in sanctity, blurring reality and fiction to ask what is real and what is good; outlandish plotting, treated with high craft, can pierce reality; rendering life's hardness creatively is what art and culture are for.

Compares the works she loves to scratch art: a black layer over rainbow colours, where what you see depends on how much and where you scratch — fully scratched, the work is complete and vivid; partly scratched, it already shows something — unlike works that present everything on the surface; she likes work with a layer to scratch.

Asks audiences to come to the screenings with as little prior information as possible — a little curiosity is enough, since a film is best met knowing nothing — and wants to hear each person's reaction, including dislike and why, comparing it to the moment right after a music video goes live.

Calls films and music her bread and water and rejects the question of why an art director makes music as ignorant: composers are artisans focused on their craft, planners see the whole — different talents; music changes any image completely and reaches people more primally than sight; she says she entered entertainment to release the music she wants, with art direction merely the bridge for her talent and visuals auxiliary to music; she need not compose, since composing would confine her to her own style, whereas selecting lets her range across styles.

Explains drawing a single flower for the curation: films made by others are like beautiful flowers she wishes she owned — they end too soon, linger long, and send you looking for the next one; this fleeting preciousness is, for her, the aesthetic of film.

The presentation's credits list her as Chief Creative Director, with a named creative director, assistant director and planners, and two outside studios credited for design, motion and 3D production — documenting a directing role over a credited team rather than sole authorship.

Introduces the rebrand as reshaping the whole brand system (company and label) and designing the new building to carry the same message; states that a good brand embodies the process of building the attitude the company expects, that space shapes attitude, and that she wanted to show how a philosophy of graphics translates into a philosophy of space.

Explains the identity as derived from the company's core and values rather than decoration: music is the starting point, so a blank musical staff in silence becomes the company's 'sheet music', notes become standards and chords; the compressed staff forms a horizontal line connecting two vertical bars — not a static symbol but one designed to change, extend and connect; an accent colour signals a forward-leaning, challenge-welcoming attitude, and the flexibility carries into the building and future applications.

Describes the office as designed to change corporate culture and ways of working along with the brand: borrowing the idea of the 'hyper nomad', she reasoned that space elicits action, so space should change first; offices should be places where people 'come together' rather than are 'placed together'; the project's motto was that the company might move tomorrow but people should be comfortable today; with teams forming per project, fixed placement was judged inefficient.

Says the interior prioritised structure and function over any individual's taste, aiming for spaces that are simple and visually appealing yet optimised for each function by eliminating forced decoration.

Details function-led decisions: a grid of movable racks and modular walls so floors can be reconfigured; identical floor structures so locations are easy to remember; free seating by default with lockers and app-based reservations; zoned lighting control; chairs chosen after tests; a dramatic ceiling chosen not for looks but to prevent shadows on desks; high colour-rendering lights to reduce eye strain.

Closes by stating that every choice, however small, was deliberated because small choices add up to good branding, and that good space branding is not decorating a space but creating the desired attitude — the goal being the most efficient and reasonable office culture.

locator: Q&A 'NewJeans went against the girl-crush trend'
claim: Says distinctive success is hard to achieve by repeating others' methods; as planner and producer she put into NewJeans everything she had wanted to improve over twenty years in the industry, which she says was possible only because management and producing were integrated in one role.
Describes weighing, as a producer, how leading young artists would be good for their lives, and wanting to propose an alternative artist–company relationship as a new business model.
Names her formative references as reading (Chekhov, Shakespeare, Kafka), late-night films, and records — Giorgio Moroder, Francis Lai, Antônio Carlos Jobim — rather than idol pop.

Says she had no interest in idols before joining SM — her Korean-pop listening was older acts (빛과소금, 산울림, 김현철) and indie — and that she joined SM to put a different idea to work inside the biggest market.

Argues culture is something that moves people and is made by people; being dazzled by the word 'industry' and losing that origin is foolish; impressive-sounding systems can be empty wordplay; intangible value is easily neglected because it is invisible, yet the decisive changes have come from it.

Reads the answer cut from the JoongAng interview: philosophy and art are usually seen as the opposite of business, and capital-shy art fades in reality; she has long wanted to join the two; capital markets pay attention only to what earns, so it mattered that NewJeans made money — with capital, intangible aesthetics and philosophy get attention and can flourish; she wants to see how far pursuing entertainment's original joy, while producing results that shine as business, can go.

Recounts early SM conditions: no design department or system; she first had to design from photos others had taken, then began choosing photographers so she could direct stylists, then asked to direct styling and was refused; idols were then dismissed by fashion magazines; she was directing stylists by the Girls' Generation period but at times lost music-video authority.

Explains choosing in-house over freelance work: a freelancer works in their own style on limited parts, while an in-house director can set direction across everything and knows the company's reality; even when hiring freelancers, direction must come from inside. Pop art, she says, is both beautiful and awful, and the job is to walk that line.

On director Shin Woo-seok: she did not instruct him because his work should not be tampered with; her direction persuaded him and their sensibilities aligned. After the success, other companies asked him for a 'Ditto season 2' — she argues that rushing after a hit makes you second or third, and that once a trend hardens, pop culture moves to a new one.

Says culture must keep changing flexibly, which is why she made the late SM logo flexible and wanted the same for HYBE's slogan; questions the idea of putting 'technology' into people and culture; wants to join art and business, which she says nobody had done well.
States that she made the SM logo and the HYBE logo; the name HYBE was not hers, but the slogan was, and she put her hopes for the company into it.

Says that when attacked, one cannot keep refuting claims in words; one has to prove things through results, actions and what is visibly real — the finished work shows itself differently and people can tell. She calls work a process of proving oneself.

Says she did not always do work because she loved it; a sense of responsibility to do assigned work well came first, and completing work required a kind of loyalty to it, which turns finishing a task into seeing what larger thing the work could achieve.
Says NewJeans mattered to her because there was a clear necessity for why the project had to be done and why a label had to be created — something to show the world through it.

Says NewJeans was drawn up from the start as a picture of five: appearance, sound, colour, style and stage movement were all designed on the premise of five members, which is why it resonated and took one complete shape; the group is 'full' only when each member's colour and sound interlock.

Proposes a new management model with much shorter contracts than the customary seven years and a revised standard contract: the standard form still has loopholes because it was written from the employer's side, minors are often told to sign if they want to be idols, and drafters do not know working practice; she wants to propose changes, which is part of why she wants a label. She wondered aloud whether her dispute is part of a paradigm shift toward more advanced practice.
Wants a company in which idols and the company need each other: people should work together because they want to and need each other, not because a long contract holds them.
Says her next project will not be a girl group: if she makes a group soon it will be a boy group, which she calls her usual order — a boy group first, then perhaps a girl group.
Says she can see what is missing in the current market and wants to prepare in her own way and show it properly, filling the empty spots in the market.
Says the label is not simply about making money: if the work is done well, money follows naturally.

A music-business trade outlet frames her plan as a 'new management model' (shorter terms, closing standard-contract loopholes) and sets her boy group against a wider industry return to boy-group investment, citing moves by HYBE and US labels.
Says she has no reason to build a rival to NewJeans; judged by her creative style and the sequence of her past work, a boy group simply comes next.

Reports a flood of direct-message applicants and proposals for entirely new, non-idol kinds of work, which she is reviewing; says her real goal goes beyond one group: a company that is fun and creatively interesting.

The launch videos speak in fragments of a fictional world rather than explanations: the first is a woman on the phone in French saying she is in front of the record shop, that much is coming and the listener will like it; another shows a 'WANTED' billboard with a young man's face and the label website, seeking males born 2008–2013; another starts on one dancer under red light and pulls back to reveal different people dancing throughout a building.

Reports that clues to the first boy group were scattered through the 23 videos as easter eggs (a passing glance, melodies hidden under city noise, unexplained numbers on walls), which fans treated as a deduction game.

A report describes the unannounced 3 February opening of the label's Instagram, X and website, with teasers released only through her personal account and the label channels, as aiming at an 'aesthetics of discovery' in which fans find and spread information themselves, and the videos as leaving standard K-pop label content behind through mise-en-scène and metaphorical symbols that invite interpretation.

The label opened a worldwide boy-group audition (males born 2008–2013, any nationality or residence, applications 24 February to 27 March via its website). The poster seeks a boy with pure passion for music, varied personas and unmeasured potential, says this boy will soon be known to the world, and uses a face glimpsed briefly in the launch videos.

The label said the project would leave formulaic frames and focus on the boys' own innate beauty and the musical narrative they will create; the world would watch a seed grow into a great forest, and it would release the boys' trajectories step by step, recording the group's birth like an epic.
key_term: 소년들이 가진 본연의 아름다움과 그들이 빚어낼 음악적 서사

claim: Reports that choreographers Black Q and Kim Eun-ju, who created the performances for NewJeans' 'Hype Boy', 'Ditto' and 'Super Shy', updated their social profiles to show they had joined ooak records.

A critic calls the boy group an unprecedented test: unlike at SM and HYBE she now works without a large system or capital; the industry has long debated whether NewJeans' success owed more to her planning or to HYBE's capital; and the uncertain continuation of her music partner BANA is a risk where music, visuals and performance must all align.

A business outlet notes that ten months after founding the label had disclosed nothing about its March 2026 audition and its social accounts had been silent since; it argues that the seven-year contract norm exists to recoup training investment, so her shorter-contract model will have to persuade investors, and that economies of scale make a new company's success uncertain.

After the first-instance ruling the label said it would move on as originally planned: build a stable management base, concentrate on maximising artists' value and nurturing new talent to represent K-pop, discover artists in a way only it can, and make content that inspires global fans; she would return to her main work as creator, producer and executive, answering with new music and stages rather than draining disputes.

Says she and HYBE belong on the stage of creation, not in court, and asks the industry's adults to go back to competing through music and stages; the longer disputes run, the more the artists, whom she calls the industry's protagonists, are harmed.
Says she had a creative vision when launching NewJeans that she was unable to complete.
Describes the concern she raised in 2024 as one of creative ethics, and presents raising it as a management judgment that a label head is obliged to make.

Says she will drop the 'former ADOR CEO' tag and, as head of ooak records, put all her energy into developing new artists to represent K-pop and into business in a new direction, concentrating on creative work, which she calls what she does best.

In a phone interview after the statement, says she will fund the label by attracting investment rather than relying on the put-option money, reports many domestic and foreign investment offers, and says she will review them cautiously.

Says she took the Movieland curator role because she wanted to talk about what she loves, film above all; the venue's purpose struck her as necessary even before it was explained, and she wanted to do this first, without deliberating, because it lets her show what is most like herself.
Explains why the programme poster shows a single flower rather than a bouquet: each artwork has its own specialness and preciousness, and these films are each too important to rank.

Her programme 'Flowers Kept' paired five screenings with audience talks at Movieland in Seongsu-dong: films listed as 'A Man and a Woman' (7 May), 'Splash' (15 May), 'Bad Education' (23 May), 'The 400 Blows' (29 May) and 'The Swimming Pool' (6 June). Tickets sold out quickly, and the venue warned that the talks might not end.

Says that from childhood she built a world of her own through films, music and books, and that film became a source of her creativity; the channel titles one segment as a source of inspiration she has drawn on for 40 years.
Describes her method as instinctively locating the point where the public feels something is missing but cannot say exactly what, and filling it; cites NewJeans as an example.

Says she started a label because she wanted to make music; when the fundamentals are solid they can become an industry in themselves, and those who concentrate on the essence end up changing the larger current.
key_term: 본질에 집중하는 사람이 큰 흐름을 바꿀 수밖에 없다

claim: Says an independent label was needed as a minimum protective barrier: when the power of capital tries to sway the domain of creation, someone has to block it and protect the artists; culture loses all its appeal the moment money eats into it.

Attributes NewJeans' success to essence and purity: following trends is a business of volunteering to be a late follower and staying second; she wanted to take things others had not done, minor but good enough, raise them to a major level of finish and introduce them to the public.
key_term: 마이너하지만 충분히 좋은 것을 메이저의 완성도로

claim: Asked about a proposed relocation of a national arts university, argues that such change should come from what students and members want; whatever is pushed artificially or for political reasons falls behind in culture and is shunned by the public, and discovering and supporting artists already hidden in the region matters more than administrative moves.

Argues that a region's nature and cultural environment feed creative sensibility: Seoul-based creators often find greater inspiration outside the capital, and in the digital and AI era creation and collaboration are fully possible from the regions, which should be seen as places of opportunity rather than deficit.
Advises students aiming at the entertainment industry to make content themselves and consume it actively, steadily discovering which sensations and tastes they are drawn to.

Says she wants hidden artists to be seen; as culture develops, life grows richer and healthy pleasures grow, so people can live happily without much money; she cannot satisfy everyone but wants to work out, realistically, ways for more people to feel satisfied and coexist.
Says cultural forms may differ in level but not in worth, and that people do not live by money alone.
Says culture always goes together with sociology and philosophy; it cannot exist on its own.

Says that however far times advance, clashes between established systems and new ones recur; where conditions do not change easily, resisting is necessary, whether one resists changes everything, and even resistance that fails carries meaning as a message to the world. She related this to her own industry dispute.
Says the boy group will offer a new kind of fun, different from the images she presented with girl groups.

Says she will not lean on the usual marketing that targets a particular age group and will step away from K-pop business models built on age-targeting or short-term hits, aiming for a group that appeals to people who love music and culture.
Says the debut date will be set by balancing her own concept against conditions and picking the most suitable moment; line-up and timing were not yet fixed.
Expressed an intention to enter the Japanese market and said an official announcement of some kind would come in about two months.

Says that even at SM, when she was drawing attention, she was a producer who stayed out of the spotlight: from her mid-thirties she turned down every television-appearance and advertising offer, partly by temperament and partly because such exposure felt burdensome, keeping to her creative-director role.
The preview's title quotes her saying she wanted to show good artwork to teenagers and people in their twenties, presented as the driving force that made her work.
Explains the 'everyone ok' concept as carrying two messages at once, 'everything OK!' and 'everything OK?', because presenting a double meaning sets people's imagination working.
key_term: 両義的な意味を提示すると人々は想像力を働かせます

claim: Says she had long declined such requests because she felt no need, and accepted this one for the symbolism of a project presenting today's Seoul and because of the editor-in-chief: at their first meeting his gift of hard-to-find books matched her taste precisely, showing he had studied and understood her, which made her want to work with him; she prized the speed, precision and care of the months-long production.

Asked why she keeps so many books and magazines in an age of web and social media, says content made with sincerity and good faith matters in every era and keeps its power across time; the high-quality joy that good content gives is hard to replace with anything else.

On being photographed by Song Si-young, a long-time collaborator on her visuals, says she rates highly his detached, matter-of-fact way of seeing a subject, and that his existing understanding of her made the shoot smooth.
On the navy cap at the centre of the collaboration, says she likes simple items that are practical yet let the wearer's own character show naturally.
Her message to those waiting for ooak records: whatever they are imagining, she wants to show them something beyond it.
Her Seoul guide for the issue picks a mini-theatre (Movieland, where she was guest curator in May), a vintage-furniture shop, a lifestyle shop, a Korean home-cooking restaurant and a listening space.

The Casa BRUTUS editor says Murakami Takashi introduced them; before their first meeting (March 2025, at Kaikai Kiki's Tokyo office) he studied her Instagram story highlights for days, read her taste as close to the jazz and soft-rock sensibility of Toru Hashimoto's 'Suburbia' selections yet also drawn to the cult rapper MF DOOM, and brought a hard-to-find book listing 1960s–70s records and an MF DOOM T-shirt to show how he read those opposite tastes.

Says the gift suited her far beyond 100 percent, above all because it paired seemingly opposite music; she loves indie hip-hop too, and holds that if you dig into the roots and attributes of genres that seem completely different, old and new music all connect.

Says that in naming (NewJeans and ADOR as well as ooak) she prefers intuitive names: none that needs explaining, but simple names with a good sound that land in the ear at once, not too serious and a little playful, because pursuing fun matters in entertainment and much of it has become too serious.

Explains ooak: the name came to her late at night before sleep; she liked the sense of anything and anyone being OK, so the letters carry another meaning while the word is pronounced 'OK', with the K also standing for Korea. She later learned that an early Korean company called OK Record had launched many idols and popular singers at the industry's dawn, and found its founder's working style and direction close to her own, which felt like fate.

Asked how the fictional record-shop videos were conceived, says she always starts, as with NewJeans, from what she herself wants, wants to do and would want to experience as a customer; she cannot accept selling something she would not want just because it is business, and her business philosophy is to build and sustain a company that makes things she truly wants.

Asked what partners she wants, says she does not decide in advance whom to work with: having learned much from past major problems, she will keep pursuing the work she has always done and expects unforeseen encounters to produce new collaborations.

The editor says the 'everyone ok' idea came during a May trip to Seoul to see her talk: they discussed apparel, she wanted a brand collaboration, and because she often wears a navy cap he thought of everyone, a brand rich in navy items whose designer Ryo Miyoshi he had just met.

Says she does not make goods to earn money: for each project she makes them as keepsakes that let people recall that time later and give the memory meaning, as she did for the Tokyo Dome shows, because wanting to keep important events and happy memories is close to an instinct; she and her collaborators tend to work from 'this is fun' rather than from profitability.

Describes directing the NewJeans Tokyo Dome shows: at that scale she cannot direct every shot, so she explains the overall context and intent, makes sure it is understood and then entrusts the crew, hoping they reach the angles she imagines; when a camera operator caught HANNI in an extreme close-up exactly as she had pictured, she felt the thrill of being understood without words, and such moments feed her expectations for the next job.
key_term: 言葉にしなくても伝わる

claim: Says she wants to keep working with Japanese companies and creators: Murakami Takashi worked very fast without a single problem, and crews such as the one on a NewJeans shampoo commercial in Japan seemed to enjoy their work, to be doing what they wanted and to get along; she found that professionals who share one goal and understand each other tacitly create great force.

Says she has a broad direction and a rough blueprint for ooak records but nothing concretely fixed: she works flexibly, linking whatever points, events or problems strike her as interesting to the goals she already holds to create synergy, and would welcome things starting in unexpected ways; her aim is to keep doing work everyone can enjoy.

Commenting on the issue's pre-release sales, says she finds it interesting that readers across borders respond to a candid record of the Seoul she sees and the things she likes, and that good content can be discovered and enjoyed beyond language or region, each person in their own way.
The partner brand everyone said that working with graphics it had never tried before felt fresh, and that seeing the item samples renewed its admiration for her sense.

Says she gets her thrill from how well she can work inside a given budget, which is why she does not do fine art: fine art competes with infinity, while commercial art gives deadlines and budgets, inside which she fights herself to see what comes out.
Repeats that her thrill is pushing potential as far as possible within given time and budget — the cheaper the budget, the bigger the thrill — and the host calls this a practical judgment.

Argues that few people truly have taste, because most choose among options others have already set and call that their taste without seriously questioning it; convenience is the price of the era — when finding music required effort, the effort built density of thought and action. She adds that each generation has its own strengths and weaknesses.
key_term: 취향… 남들이 정해 놓은 거 중에서 골라서

claim: Describes music as having the power to change a space: when music in her style plays, she is suddenly in a different place; she calls music the time machine humans already have, says she is especially sensitive to sound, and wants her environment shaped into the space she wants.

Recounts that a chance record purchase gave each track its own story and memory, and says that in making NewJeans she wanted listeners to have that kind of experience, because today's environment keeps people listening only to ready-made music; she wanted to show something that slips out of that environment, out of pride in her taste ('why don't people listen to this?').

Says contrasting combinations excite people — strikingly pretty members who are casual and unaffected — and that the bigger feeling comes where mismatched things meet; she thought pop culture lacked such unbalanced matching.

Gives her market analysis for NewJeans: K-pop fans would look anyway because of her name, so the gain was in drawing people like her — not interested in idols, somewhat hipster — which widens the pie arithmetically and emotionally, crossing gender, generation and genre; she judged a girl group more advantageous for that and wanted to show a girl group could earn more. The host summarises it as aesthetic judgment, audience understanding and business judgment moving together, and she agrees.
Says she is decisive and dislikes push-and-pull; she wants work decisions clear and fast and tries not to confuse others, precisely because she considers herself complicated.

Says she has long assumed that what she likes others will like, from a conviction since childhood that her eye and ear were different; although she is often seen as niche she considers herself popular — things are just not yet known, like seeds waiting to be introduced; she cites a hit producer's view that what he likes is what is popular.

Describes the unrealised original plan for NewJeans' first showcase: a large-but-intimate warehouse space, two producers DJing, the audience seated on the floor at the members' level like a traditional open-yard performance, everyone handed the same garment, because NewJeans' appeal grows the closer you meet them; staff objected on security, safety and capacity grounds. She had also once proposed a surprise live set in a club.

Says she shares the picture she is imagining with the members in real time; they add their own ideas; when their imagination drops she boosts it, and she has to do the 'crazy thing' first so others feel free to jump in.

Names improvisation as what K-pop lacks: talent is found and trained but the feeling of improvising is missing, and training processes make it hard to grow; because environment matters she wanted to be involved from training, with a stated stance — mistakes are pointed out without humiliation, wrongs are named and apologised for — and with a belief that explains why each task is done, which she says removes most frustration.

Describes the team as a community that needs goodwill loyalty; members resolve conflict in different ways, and her role is to tell them they must find their own way of resolving it — she cannot find it for them.

Says she keeps the same stance toward superiors, juniors, artists and employees; in group settings she is, if anything, harder on the most senior person so juniors can relax; her rules are not to do shabby things, to be honest, and to solve problems by talking sincerely.

Rejects cringe-inducing words such as 'healing', 'comfort' and 'warmth'; says the NewJeans plan avoided a condescending stance of giving healing — comfort is received voluntarily, not handed down — so the focus was entertaining, non-vulgar fun ('let's do cool, fun, stylish things'), from which comfort follows naturally while taste and standards seep in unnoticed.
Says that to be able to tell the industry that a practice is meaningless, she first has to succeed and then dismantle it — the first-placed has to remove the first place for people to listen.

On the Tokyo Dome solo stages: each member reinterpreted another artist's song in her own style; she expected the reaction to the Matsuda Seiko cover. Inspiration, she says, was not 'make it like that' but the singular energy that singer gave off — close to her idea of an idol — and the observation that today there is no stage for such plain, plaintive, little-decorated songs that maximise one person's charm, since current music is specialised for visuals and complex arrangement; she wanted it at Tokyo Dome rather than on a broadcast stage.

Says she walked every seating area of Tokyo Dome, including restricted-view seats, and released those seats only after deliberation because she did not want anyone neglected; seats could have been added for revenue but were not; her biggest single priority was a very large screen so back rows could see.

Describes the Tokyo Dome crew as a patchwork she assembled outside the usual concert teams — art, staging and lighting from a US team, filming from a Japanese team, music via the BANA head — directing in three languages; she singles out 'directors of directors', people above the technicians, as important and under-recognised, and credits the supporting staff and performance director for covering her absences during the turmoil.

Recounts that rehearsal time at the venue was nearly unavailable, so the members practised in a flat rented hall with the stage drawn on the floor and had only two venue rehearsals; the first technical rehearsal went badly, yet the professionals executed the show without a single mistake, including an unspoken extreme close-up she had pictured — the pleasure of working with good people.

Names her core creative circle (music-video directors, the performance director, stylist, the BANA producers, art director, photographers) and says they work with little explanation because of a shared core of taste, professional attitude and a shared cause; she pitched the label to them from the NewJeans planning stage, explaining in all-night meetings why she was making a label and what it would pursue.

Says she wanted a project in which each collaborator's portfolio is perfected while together they do something large — a natural 'new wave', as with the Nouvelle Vague or bossa nova (she cites Truffaut's The 400 Blows) — yet no one in the group ever talks about changing the world, which they find cringeworthy: they just do funny, exciting things with an unspoken expectation of the ripple.

Says the fan name felt to her like the name of a crew of friends rather than a fandom, so 'selling to the fandom' felt odd; since business still requires money to be reproduced and expanded, her answer was to give a lot of good things so that a voluntary virtuous cycle forms — idealistic, she says, but achievable.

Says she wants the process to be good as well as the result, which makes the work tiring; she works by reverse-engineering from the design only she fully knows, and the subtlety comes alive when she keeps each worker's individuality and only pinches the points they missed — otherwise everything becomes her style and the same thing comes out every time.

Describes her twenty years in K-pop as training: once imperfect, she says she has evolved toward finding ways to work enjoyably without needlessly raising voices, which she calls her task and ultimate wish.

Says she never calls weak work good; when she says 'good' in recording, it was good; she praises sparingly at work because over-praise misleads, saves warmth for private settings, and at work states clearly which direction is right, because habituation to praise or to nagging breeds ingrained bad habits.

Argues that audiences should enjoy the gradation of growth — each stage has its own virtue — and that demanding finished perfection from the start, as the K-pop idol scene tends to, throws away the audience's own pleasure; she links this to a fan culture that sees itself in a producer-like role.

Asked how inspiration translates when she neither draws nor composes, says she does not copy what she loves; it gives her an impression or feeling she wants to express, which she then renders in a different medium — visualising it, or turning it into an action, since promotion is an action that makes people experience something; music makes her picture experiences.

Distinguishes intuition from literalness: delivering something childish childishly is not intuitive; intuition contains concept and thought. Art is the maker encoding emotion and the audience decoding it; if no encoding or decoding is needed, the work is simply simple and childish; when aesthetic experience and training let the decoding happen instinctively and universally, that is truly intuitive — and that is what she wants to make.

Says she drew attention partly because people outside pop culture who felt 'only I feel this' saw her do it openly in pop culture, which made them both glad and resentful; she says she values those feelings.

Says pop culture's quality rises through delicate tuning — sometimes leaving people alone, sometimes leading — rather than propaganda; the moment you proclaim you have brought something good, culture is received with resistance; art loses its value the moment it declares itself, and becomes tacky; people who know the value never declare it.

Says making such work is why producing and management must go together: she pursues 'perfect beauty' in the sense of realising her own picture as fully as possible, which cannot happen without an exquisite combination with business — arranging for two outside IP holders to meet for a collaboration is her role, because she knows the excitement such a project creates.

Says a business partner must be won by the excitement of the project, not by 'let's do this because we'll make money'; she cites Apple as a company where someone who understood subtlety also held a firm business philosophy and could push and control density, so people accept inconvenience — which she calls art; spending is an implicit game, and people need pride to be 'robbed pleasantly'.

Calls her work 'making pretty trash': nobody needs an album to live, but things that make you feel good just by looking enrich life; changing small everyday moments is pop culture's role, mission and power.

Explains the instrumental interlude on a NewJeans record by reference to a bossa-nova album that casually includes instrumentals: an unhurried interlude signals 'we are not in a rush because we pursue something', which gives listeners a sense of richness; creating an artistic atmosphere inside idol pop matters, and once familiar it becomes natural.

Recounts choosing between piano and flute versions of the interlude: a collaborator brought a flute version unasked; she worried it sounded old-fashioned, but it was more nostalgic, which fit the record's direction, so the flute won; she describes good work as each director's ego fitting exactly into its position and meshing, which is where completeness clicks.

Says each music-video director has a distinct style, so she gives direction differently to each — as with each member — not out of courtesy but because it makes the work more fun and makes it burst; inducing that is her role.

Names her greatest frustration as carefully made production being crushed in the business process; business is timing and fit with media, placed at the right moment by a designer who sees the whole. Home runs happen when skilled people meet by chance — she values chance — and her aim is to control the work so it yields value even without a home run.

Qualifies her own thesis: integrating management and producing is not universally better — some people flourish when the two are separated because they complement each other; it is that she, being who she is, needs to do it all, and arguing it as a binary misses the point; letting each person work the way their potential bursts is what respects artists, workers and culture.
Says her approach is to make the least-regret choice at each moment; even when the outcome is not what she wanted, she has found it flows somewhere meaningful.

Says people who listened to her shared playlists sensed from them that she loves music and pursues newness, and some offered to help her for that reason; she calls this the power of taste — and beyond it, the exchange that a shared taste creates.

Describes her musical taste as mellow: even fast tracks should feel like bedroom pop; funky or psychedelic but always mellow; melancholy but with brightness inside, languid rather than gloomy — 'the sadness of a major key rather than a minor key' — and the catharsis when two opposite poles strike a subtle balance, like laughing and crying at once.

Names the first music she recognised as her own taste — bossa nova (Jobim, Astrud Gilberto's voice) — followed by Francis Lai's film music and Giorgio Moroder's Italian disco; she liked French, Italian and Brazilian music, noting European-style music was popular when she was young and that her listening was not chosen to seem unusual.

Says she learned art largely from large museum-archive art books; a reproduction in such a book moved her more than seeing the original at the Louvre, and she kept a newspaper page because a Sistine Chapel restoration image was printed beautifully on the paper's tinted stock — while the site itself later felt underwhelming.

Says she put bossa nova into every university assignment; she values it because it can absorb every genre like a template, yet played cheaply it becomes endlessly cheap, while played with density it is the height of refined beauty — the same form can sound monotonous or dense.

Says she likes the cultural currents of the 1950s–70s in music and art, singling out 1969 as a year when minor genres such as bossa nova and cool jazz reached the top of the charts and pop culture was rich — the last moment a romantic revolution seemed possible — and notes that music is closely tied to political and social change; current bedroom pop carries those traits lightly, but she does not like only light things.

Says moody Italian lounge and 1970s Italian film music, B-movies and melancholic films 'raised' her sensibility and creative desire — not as 'I must make this music', but as a sensibility she wants to express in some form; inspiration, she says, is reinterpreted and embodied.

Gives an SM-era example: a photo shoot with three SM artists was planned from a single song — the song was the real protagonist. The emotion she wanted was the in-between feeling before a strong emotion, 'a feeling only I know' that, when someone else knows it too, is how people fall in love; so the subjects should share emotion subtly without going too deep, and the shoot should leave them a good memory — her way of visualising a song.

Director Shin Woo-seok says that at their first meeting Min talked about a horizontal relationship between fans and idols and said she wanted the release to be a gift to fans; that conversation made him want to tell a story about the fan-idol relationship, which is why he took on what became his first music video.

Shin says she wanted a new kind of music video and, so as not to constrain his thinking, mentioned only one image she had pictured on hearing the song - a deer standing alone in a snowfield - adding that it need not be used; she then gave him full authority over the scenario and the direction.

Shin says that while Ditto was in progress she arranged meals with the NewJeans members and invited him to their practice room so that he would know their characters; meeting them several times shaped his OMG scenario about young people whose free expression is judged and narrowed by outside readings.
Shin says the bigger decision was ADOR's, not his: his formally and narratively radical approach could have been a burden from a producer's standpoint, yet ADOR accepted it readily.

Shin states that he conceived and wrote the Ditto scenario without interference and that its devices - the camera-holding character Hee-su (named to echo the fan-club name), the school uniforms and the camcorder - were his own.

Shin says he hesitated when she proposed that he make an idol music video, and agreed because he trusted her: he knew her as someone who kept proposing new directions in the scene, saw that in NewJeans' earlier videos, and felt she clearly respected creators.

Shin gives his own reasons for OMG's casting and narration: cartoonist Lee Mal-nyeon (Chimchakman) as an adult who looks at the members' imagination without prejudice, and Hanni, whose first language is not Korean, voicing the opening narration as a story of idols reshaped passively by public standards.

Shin says he had understood that she usually plans music videos herself or is deeply involved, but that she appeared to respect his established way of working; in person she trusted her own choices and pushed them without hesitation, and their conversations about a healthy fan-idol relationship became the basis of his scenario.

Shin says the deer in the school corridor stands for the ideal friend idols would want, names the Greek myth of Circe's pigs as a seed of the scenario, and says he had never seen the 'Whispering Corridors' films viewers compared it to.
Hanni says Min checks each point of their concept carefully, and recalls her explaining that things once popular or fashionable come back and are liked again in the present.
Hyein says Min has told them that a person's charm comes through when they are honest, and that Min talks with them candidly, so the members also communicate openly with her.

ADOR performance director Kim Eun-ju says that from the trainee period to debut Min kept giving her feedback that the performance should not be boxed in, should attempt something new and avoid the predictable, while still incorporating mass appeal.

Kim says she was stuck after a first full draft of the 'Hype Boy' choreography; Min phoned to say she could take her time, that the chorus point did not have to be a triangle formation, and suggested rendering the trendiest dance style a little more easily. The final chorus dropped the triangle for members pushing past one another with upper- and lower-body groove and room for individual expression, and it spread as a meme.

In the label's announcement of V's solo album, says she received the offer in late 2022 and hesitated over scheduling but was drawn by his attitude, passion and a vocal tone she had not known well; asks listeners to focus on the music, which combines his taste with songs she wanted to propose, favouring music they wanted to make and that could be carried off well over familiar styles.
NME, citing Big Hit Music's confirmation to Sports Donga, reports that Min would lead V's solo album project, including the music, choreography and promotion style.

Says she wanted the overall mood of V's album to focus on the plain, understated side beneath his glamour; she had a musical style she wanted to propose to him, built the tracklist from it with his vocal tone and style in mind, played it to him, and they agreed at once. Presents 'Rainy Days' as the album's intro, with plain yet muffled vocals and visuals.

V says he contacted Min first because he wanted someone who would maximise his own taste and sensibility; they shared opinions down to small details, the work felt like mutual enjoyment rather than forced alignment, and he says the ideas he actively proposed were taken up.
V says the album title 'Layover' was decided after many conversations with Min about the album's direction.
V describes the album as removing the glamorous elements of the stage to show the colour he has as a person.

Jang Ji-min recalls joining SM's visual directing team as its most junior member, with Min - then holding the title 과장 - leading the team; at a time when 'visual directing' was an unfamiliar term, the team's work ran from album design to artists' visual storytelling and included going to music-video sets.

Jang says Min, who joined SM as a graphic designer, told her she had asked whether she could go to photo shoots and gradually built up visual planning from there; Jang saw her direct on music-video sets and return to the office at dawn to review and retouch the footage and photos.
Jang says Min told her she had to be proactive, and describes Min as someone who worked out what she herself could do and acted on it immediately.

At her solo showcase Tiffany says she had often taken part in visual directing and styling before, but as a solo newcomer wanted to put all her energy into singing and dancing; she credits 'director (이사) Min Hee-jin' with the concept, video and styling, which she says produced images not seen before.

Dispatch reports that styling for SHINee's 2015 album 'Odd' (title track 'View') was handled by director Min Hee-jin, who had worked with SHINee since their debut; the teaser styling was relaxed - loose T-shirts with denim.

As SM's visual directing team leader, explains Girls' Generation's 'The Boys' stage costumes: each member's own taste was reflected while her strengths were maximised, because showing nine members' different strengths in one look felt limiting; costumes were varied anew for each stage to reveal each member's appeal and the song's several images, and she expected the accumulated variations to highlight the group's ability to interpret songs.

Says hand-work raises costume cost and reworking luxury-collection garments raises it further, but the first criterion is how well a costume fits the group's colour, the members' traits and the album concept; price comes second.

Describes how Girls' Generation and f(x) costumes are produced: separate makers are commissioned by garment type (skirts to a skirt specialist, trousers to a trouser specialist), garments take about three days, and stylists and assistants then work through the night attaching trims and details.
Names the 'The Boys' outfits as Girls' Generation's best costumes: she liked rendering a medieval style luxuriously, with a dramatic feel.
Says there are always regrets fans never see - a shoulder that should have been wider, a fabric whose buttons do not close - because materials and time are limited.

Says the 'The Boys' costumes were made by actively reflecting each member's taste so that what she likes and what suits her would stand out, and that afterwards, for 'Twinkle', the members took an active part in styling and responses have been improving.

At SHINee's 'Dream Girl' preview, says the costumes reflect SHINee's identity of making popular music that always aims to be fresh, carry many dreamlike yet deliberate odd devices, and were designed to break the prejudices and misconceptions people hold about SHINee.

At the same event SM producing head Lee Sung-soo (이성수) presented the album's two chapters as one combined concept and said many linking devices - puzzles in the music, visuals and lyrics - were hidden across them.

Says SHINee was conceived as an idol group that does not look like idols, a group meant to step outside the SM mould; unstandardised freedom and an artist-like, artistic image are its basic visual concept.

Says jacket and teaser images stand for an album's and a group's identity, so she deliberates over them and tries not to miss even small things in the frame: every visible element carries meaning - in a 'Romeo' image, the black tape on Key's shoe sole and the folded carpet were deliberately staged.
Says the third album's images gave form to thoughts she sensed in each member through everyday conversation, hiding what SHINee wanted to say in each image like a riddle for the public to decode.

SM's comeback announcement says f(x)'s 'Pink Tape' art film was a project planned by art director Min, who handles SM's concept planning, made with film-department students and directed and shot by 민제홍, 정우성 and 이성은 as a new form of graphic visual work with dreamlike images and narration.

W Korea published a pictorial of Taemin (SHINee), Krystal (f(x)) and Kai (EXO) titled 'Daisy Illusive', captioned on its Facebook page as three muses who entered creative director Min Hee-jin's frame.

The Kim Jun-won (Glen Check) x Krystal (f(x)) single 'I Don't Wanna Love You' was released as one concept spanning music, music video and photobook rather than as a vocal feature; Kim wrote, composed and produced the music, and the visual art was by SM creative director Min.
projects: Kim Jun-won x Krystal I Don't Wanna Love You

claim: The project's visual art (credited to Min) was shown as an exhibition in two Seoul venues with deliberately different presentations - Mudaeryuk in Hongdae (18-26 February 2017) and Boon the Shop in Cheongdam (to 12 March) - with a 100-copy limited art book sold only at the second venue.
projects: Kim Jun-won x Krystal I Don't Wanna Love You

claim: Introduces herself as SM's visual & art director who works as a graphic designer, and says she came to take on album design and various other jobs so that the concepts she designed would be expressed more clearly.

Says she majored in visual design, gained about a year at an advertising company through a student internship while still in her third year, and joined SM - her first employer after graduation - through open recruitment, attracted by album design; her lack of interest in pop music made the job more intriguing, and she wanted to show the public something new.

Describes a consistent, slightly languid personal listening style across genres: Antonio Carlos Jobim and Francis Lai, 1960s-70s Italian sounds, Brazilian music (Daniel Taubkin, Baden Powell), Giorgio Moroder recalled through Daft Punk, and Korean acts including Lee Byung-woo, Junggigo and Jazzyfact.

Says her team was a new department when she joined; she saw album design not as decorating albums prettily but as carrying the musician's or production's intention and interpretation, and working that way gradually created things that had not existed. Once an attempt succeeds it becomes systematised, but nothing changes if you keep still - you have to speak up and put the idea into practice.

Says perseverance matters most at work; because others do not move at her pace she learned to wait for the right moment, and for every project she asks herself whether she did her best in the time given.

Says that after she proposed an overall concept the company entrusted her with general visual directing including stage outfits; she disliked the split between album concept and stage costume and built a process linking concept, stage and everything else - dating this to Super Junior's 'Sorry Sorry', Girls' Generation's 'Gee', and SHINee, f(x) and EXO from their debuts.

Describes how she briefs stylists: from the start of album preparation she explains the target concept and ideas that would maximise it, then proposes and orders the core items that anchor the concept (white T-shirt and jeans, coloured skinny jeans, the 'Tell Me Your Wish' uniforms, f(x)'s school uniforms); the stylists return a concrete production plan, the two sides develop it back and forth, and making the clothes is the stylists' job.

Says showing the concept comes first and the on-stage selling point second: for SHINee's debut song 'Replay' she planned with Taemin in advance that he would pull up the hood of his spangled hoodie at a focal point of the dance - a small direction fans came to wait for.

Says she leads album-jacket shoots because they are her plans and sometimes does the styling herself (as for f(x)'s 'Pink Tape' jacket and art film); collaboration is hard because people see the same thing differently, and it is a problem when a concept is misunderstood or comes out other than intended, since the company needs the initial concept realised.

Says planning for the next album starts near the end of each promotion; she wanted a romantic f(x), sketched everything from video to album design quickly after hearing the title song, felt a matching video was needed, and told the company she wanted to make a film as a new concept; the symbolic idea was a pink VHS, which led to the title and design 'Pink Tape'.

Says the boundary of her job matters little: if something seems needed she proposes and makes it, despite the complications of stepping outside her territory; music-video production was not her duty, yet for SHINee's 'Dream Girl' she suggested the Digipedi team to the company, and as a graphic worker she can approach video from an angle different from video specialists.

Names the image she always wants from f(x) as a 'bizarre beauty' - an atypical beauty - and says that for 'Pink Tape' she wanted to unravel f(x)'s own love story: every first love looks ordinary from outside but has a private way only its owner knows, which she wanted to visualise in a unique way.

Explains Pink Tape's look: outfits that only borrow a uniform's nuance to convey first-love freshness, an Asian touch in set, hair and make-up, a languid and melancholy mood, old sunshine pop played during the shoot, and the idea of gathering a strange omnibus of stateless, multinational students into an odd pink tape.

Says Pink Tape was made deliberately simply: as a first attempt it could not have a large budget, and budget is not proportional to result; for the director she needed someone who fully understood her aim and was new and interested in the work rather than money, and she chose a film-department student whose coursework she had seen, whose fellow students then joined.

Names light, sound and smell as the three most important elements in directing an atmosphere in any space, with light and sound especially important in video; on a low budget, how well such basic elements are applied decides the result.

Says the art film's overall mood came out somewhat brighter than everyone intended, but judges that acceptable given that f(x) are pop artists; thanks producer Lee Soo-man and the CEO for trusting her unconditionally on a first project.

Explains EXO's 'Growl' concept as street-based: on hearing the song she was sure it had to unfold in school uniforms; the first album was set in a school (cram-school references, notebooks, graduation photos) and the next song extended to the streets, linking boys' daily life from school to after school within one album; she wanted a light, student-like take on hip-hop and R&B rather than a showy one.

Defends shooting the 'Growl' jacket in a real neighbourhood alley with shop and construction signs left in: she wanted to show reality as it is and found it inversely fun to put fantasy-like idols into real settings; since the public mostly sees idols dressed up, she wanted to show that reality itself is beautiful, valuing sincerity, and printed photos of neighbourhood children and dogs as resting pages in the album.

According to the fan translation - on a line the translator marked as uncertain - EXO's premise of superpowered boys from 'EXO planet' was producer Lee Soo-man's idea, which she found creative but worried could feel distant.

Says she first made EXO's own symbol and character with planets and meteors as motifs, varying the symbol with the group's situation (for the current release, 'kiss' as a heart and 'hug' as a circle), and that the concept clicked when she asked what twelve boys who had crash-landed from an alien planet would do on Earth.

Says a special collaboration was planned and prepared alongside EXO's first album: since 'Growl' was expressed through school and street looks, she thought it fitting to work with a street label, and four collaboration shops themed on the album were prepared with a local street brand, with traces of the members hidden in the stores.

Mentions an SM special compilation planned early in 2013 for the fifth anniversary of 10 Corso Como, in which indie artists with distinct personalities reinterpreted SM songs, and says she was glad it went smoothly from the DJ line-up to the launch party.
Wishes people's perspectives on pop culture would diversify, invoking the saying that one sees only as much as one knows: a wide field of vision lets you see and enjoy more.

Architect Kim Sejoong says FHHH FRIENDS, COM and HYBE's CBO Min formed a 'Spatial Experience Design Group' that began with a historical survey of the existing office: how it had developed and where it should go next.

Yoon Hanjin says that rather than simply making decisions as coordinator of HYBE's rebranding, Min wanted to work hands-on, and that she wanted not a comfortable, problem-free office but a space with a strong message.

Yoon says the decision to customise furniture from an existing industrial system (FURSYS), using a bent pipe and bolts as base elements rather than a wholly new design, was taken together with the CBO, and frames it as an interpretation of the industrial system rather than a compromise.

The architects describe the 300-unit grid, the ceiling-hung infrastructure and the mobile racks as their own design reasoning, including their view that the common 'nomad office' idea was ornamental and that an active, systematic nomadism needed resizable racks and assemble-to-need tables.

Project credits list Min Heejin (HYBE) as Chief Brand Officer and as a member of the Spatial Experience Design Group with Yoon Hanjin, Kim Sejoong, Han Joowon and Shin Donghoon (HYBE, assistant director); signage is credited to 'HYBE CBO office / CRAFIK & Leepublic'; design ran August 2019 to August 2020 and construction August 2020 to March 2021.

In HYBE's brand presentation video - her first public appearance since 2019 - she introduced the new headquarters under a 'Hyper Nomad' concept (knowledge workers who create new markets and paradigms), with varied spaces matched to work needs and natural gathering instead of a fixed layout, and said good spatial branding aims to create an attitude, hoping a more original and efficient working culture would take root.
