claim: HYBE announced the new label ADOR with Min as CEO, with its own music-producing and creative teams and plans for new ventures across production, business and marketing; its first girl group, planned for 2022 around members chosen in the 2019 'Plus Global Audition', would be produced under her direction across the whole process.

In the founding release, says she is ready to bring another change to the music industry through the new label and will present artist IP and content that show ADOR's own philosophy, without fear of new challenges.

NewJeans' app 'Phoning', launched on 25 July 2022 by ADOR with Weverse, is built on the concept of members and fans sharing one phone: live streams arrive like incoming video calls, finished lives sit in a missed-calls list, and the app has chat, a photo album and a calendar with entries the members add themselves, aiming at a friend- or crew-like relationship beyond artist and fan.

NewJeans shared a Vogue Korea New Year cover shoot in hanbok and modern clothes through a new account on 18 December 2024; the members were presented by their personal names rather than the group name, and Min was credited - allkpop says as director of the shoot.
Says the SHINee third-album work drew fresh, fun subculture out and popularised it, and was made with newcomers who had sense and inventive ideas rather than with famous artists or photographers.

Director Shin Woo-seok says that, as before, he could only thank the producer for the creative freedom given, and that he expects it will be hard ever again to meet a producer who trusts creators this much.

Shin says he first declined the new NewJeans videos and accepted because the project became an Apple 'Shot on iPhone' collaboration, and that he wrote the ETA scenario around what only such a project could say (the phone's role in modern life, rumour) — the scenario reasoning is his.
Shin says the cameo of an internationally famous actor was secured with his letter and materials and with Min's efforts to make it happen; the actor appeared for the role regardless of screen time.

Shin says he made the members observers rather than leads in one video, expecting criticism, because every track on the EP had a member-centred video and one track focusing on the song would help the set as a whole; he also used top lighting that shadows faces — a choice hard to make in idol videos — and thanks the producer and fans for accepting such attempts.

Says that before NewJeans' launch she spent a long time weighing what the first content should be — the impression of the first photo, whether video or photo would hit harder, the most effective release time — noting that people perceive content differently at night and during the day.

Explains releasing a music video first, without teasers: the members were unrevealed and even their number unknown, so they used that as an advantage — the more you conceal, the more curiosity — and a video came first because the feeling she wanted would not come across in stills; appreciation is stronger through several senses at once.
Calls her approach designing the whole experience: not only creating content but deciding how it is presented, simultaneously with making it, because the first impression is extremely important.

Says she values fun above meticulousness and wants the whole lead-up to a release to be enjoyable; on the second EP the order of the videos made for every track was crucial — a teaser for the last track first, then the first track's video — planned to induce particular audience reactions, which she enjoyed watching unfold as imagined.

Says she is not confined to a genre and prefers music that cleverly mixes genres; 'Ditto' was chosen not for its genre but because it was moving and fit the mood and intent of the album she wanted to release that winter; she now trusts her own feeling about whether a song will make it — meaning whether it touches the heart rather than its commercial prospects.

Says her strength as a producer who does not compose is choosing songs as if painting a picture in her head — she pictures a scene on hearing a song; for school uniforms she starts from the basics by asking what the original form of a school uniform is, because 'Ditto' expresses a natural, universal feeling; she chose the uniform type after reading the director's script.

Describes her role as gathering and integrating each specialist's own idea of quality, extracting and elevating the essence, keeping their creativity while trimming the excess she considers unnecessary, and refining toward the highest completeness as she judges it.

Rejects the idea that she is driven by retro or by one trend: people are drawn to universal things, what was liked in the past is not so different from what is liked now, only the methods of expression change with the times; so she is neither attached to the past nor preoccupied with trends, and aims for something like a childhood treasure box — timeless, always pleasant, not outdated.

Says she chose 'Hype Boy' for her vision of the group, made its video in four versions to maximise the song's impression, and judged that its unusual emotional chord needed choreography unlike typical precise, synchronised group dance, following the groove naturally — which requires enjoyment; she wanted the members carefree and age-appropriate rather than moving for business.

Names naturalness as the difference from conventional K-pop, but says true naturalness cannot be staged: it comes from how the members spend their time and practise off camera, so the environment must be right; naturalness is a strength but cannot be the concept, because making naturalness a concept would be artificial.

Says she told the young members that working with her is like studying together — a seven-year contract like high school plus university, with staff as good teachers and professionals they would not meet at school — and that she dislikes the term 'idol' as now used, as a job title rather than its original meaning, hoping NewJeans breaks the stereotypes.

Says casting weighed whether the five members' moods matched and whether their values were broadly aligned, as with her staff; because young people's tastes are still forming, she cast for budding potential rather than finished qualities, not mechanically for looks or singing.

Explains the bunny light stick: NewJeans had no logo but needed a unifying symbol; just before sleep, the letters N and J in her head became a bunny face — the members resembled bunnies, bunnies are prolific (a hope for a growing fanbase), so the face stands for both members and fans; removable eyes let each fan customise their own bunny, and the large head reads as a heart — 'my face, but also my heart'.
Says the better they do the more pressure they feel, so with each album she tries to return to the excitement of first planning the content, music and visuals.

Says most label heads came from making music or from management, while a content maker becoming a CEO is rare; even without composing, deciding which music to select and what finished product to build proposes a very different production method — different casting and training, built from what she had thought about over twenty years, prepared for about two years.

Says that because the idol industry works with very young people, she regards the process for them as upbringing rather than work, feels a producer's responsibility accordingly, and spent time getting close to each trainee individually.

Says 'artist' is one of the words she most likes being called, and that she wants to build a process in which the members naturally become artists — raw but hard-working, so that if they enjoy the work a very different vibe will emerge.

Says she thought proving herself would end after a few successes, but it never ends and the barriers grow, so it becomes a game of beating herself; what it needs most is a heavy sense of responsibility, which is what lets one take risks steadily — persuading the people who must do new work and preparing alternatives as insurance in case it fails — together with a fighting spirit.

Explains the name ooak as saying 'OK' not to anything, but meaning something special when it is said, while staying open to every kind of content and business that moves in a direction everyone can agree on.

Says the initials do not stand for one fixed phrase: she chose them intuitively because the letter sequence looks good and can carry many readings (e.g. 'only one', 'always known'), weighing the graphic combination of the letters together with the direction of meaning; the different logos mean different things but connect; birds stand for a freedom everyone recognises, and the logo is hand-drawn to express it as freely as possible.

Says the launch video was meant to give a sense of direction while the business blueprint is still vague: it uses subtle imagery from the record shops she loved as a child, which sold clothes and their own goods alongside records — a dream space showing a business built on what she likes but meant to be loved by others, not a plan to run a shop.

Says dinosaurs came to her intuitively as a simple symbol for the boy group, in the way the bunny worked for NewJeans; two long-time directors made a playful video from her story on a whim, with mutual respect.

Says the label's teasers were made with directors she has worked with for years, who helped like friends; what matters most is sincerity — the people in sync with her do not put money first but ask why they have to create something and how to make it interesting, and that is how long collaborations formed.

Says she had declined earlier cover offers from Korean fashion magazines because she weighs the reason and meaning for doing something and could not see why she should be on a fashion cover; she accepted this one because conveying her way of living interested her and the magazine was one she loved.
Describes her lifelong creative orientation as frame-breaking: whatever new thing she makes has to get past an existing frame, which is what always made the work hard.

Recounts that before leaving SM she proposed giving up her registered-director post to run a subsidiary for a new girl-group plan, judging that something new could not be built inside SM's existing organisation and that taking the CEO title would not change that; she declined an offer of the SM presidency for the same reason.

Says her first HYBE assignment was the group's branding as Big Hit became a holding company, and that she insisted on also taking on the headquarters building, knowing it would be tiring, because giving the company's attitude a physical form mattered for the work's completeness.

Recounts the original set-up for HYBE's first girl group: launching a girl group straight from a label whose fandom (BTS) is largely female was judged risky, so a separate women's label using Source Music's existing trainees was planned for speed, with work split three ways — her creative direction, the chairman's music, Source Music's management; she initially resisted because she prefers to carry a plan through from start to finish herself.

Gives her trainee-selection criteria: of the existing female trainees she found only one (Minji) she could select; the others needed much more training, were too old for the plan, or did not match her sensibility.

Explains that casting depends on branding because applicants read a label's brand before applying: with no senior artists to feature (the usual audition poster shows seniors' faces and the company name) and a weakly branded host label, she branded the audition itself around the planned group's direction — Hanni came through it — and further scouting ran under the banners 'Min Hee-jin's girl group' and HYBE's first girl group, counting on curiosity about her unusual pairing with a boy-band label.

Says that around 2020–21, while the joint project stalled, she already had her own planning document and songs including 'Attention' and 'Hype Boy' in hand, and considered the direction settled even though HYBE's side was not enthusiastic about it.

Recounts insisting that ADOR's first public announcement (late 2021) state that the group would be all new members and all teenagers; asked to keep this ambiguous, she saw no point in announcing at all, since the purpose was to end public confusion about which group was hers; she also went on a TV talk show she would normally avoid to front the launch herself.

Argues that a multi-label system only makes sense if each label keeps its own character: a holding company that centralises shared functions (IT, HR, PR) finds control easy, but labels may need different PR and personnel approaches; if they are not allowed to differ, it would be more honest to run one company like SM or YG.

Asked how a multi-label group should improve, says the top decision-maker should stay above the labels rather than personally produce some of them: when the chair produces certain labels, others start courting favour and outsiders sort labels into favoured and unfavoured children — human nature, she says, and not unique to HYBE (SM had similar problems) — whereas a detached top lets labels compete autonomously and grow healthily.

Distinguishes shared surface elements, which anyone may use (her example: straight hair), from imitating a whole production formula; when easy copying succeeds, under-resourced creators conclude there is no point in thinking — just copy — so everything converges on one look, which harms the original, the imitator and, in the long run, the industry; raising the issue is therefore in the business's interest.

Explains that by a production formula she means a flow of branding moves rather than any single element — for example an audition poster's tone and manner, holiday shoots in hanbok at a royal palace, a first appearance at a fashion-brand event — and that when such a flow is replicated the original's uniqueness turns into a standard template; a group owner, she holds, should stop such replication internally, since it is discourteous to the earlier act and does the later one no good.

Explains NewJeans' album packaging: albums now carry many photos, so putting every member into one package would make it as thick as a dictionary, while CD prices have stayed around 15,000–16,000 won for decades as costs rose; versions are therefore split by member and each made with care; she dislikes random packing but uses it because fixed member versions would expose the members' relative popularity, which she wants to avoid; she says she reviews everything from A to Z as responsibility for something designed with intent, not as micromanagement.

Criticises push-out sales and random-photocard tactics: once some sellers use them nobody can tell what drives the numbers, the market turns abnormal and even share prices are distorted by charts that only rise, while costs shift to fans (lucky draws, repeat purchases for fansigns) and artists are worn down by endless fansign events; she says she started NewJeans partly to show success is possible without such tricks — from the start she wanted to see how far a clean approach could go.

Says NewJeans' first public appearance at a Chanel event was not planned: the fashion event happened to fall before the first music-show broadcast and she chose to embrace it as unusual and fun; she adds that the group's advertisers came through her own relationships and their curiosity about the project, not through the parent company.

States that her first duty was as CEO of ADOR, a separately incorporated label, which can conflict with the role of a parent company's subsidiary head — loyalty to the parent sometimes means acting against the label's artists; separate incorporation exists so that the label's interest comes first (otherwise it would be a team inside the parent), and she argues that a label left to work independently returns more to the parent and its shareholders through results.

Argues that loyalty words such as 'betrayal' belong to groups held together by personal allegiance, not to a joint-stock company: a manager proves herself with numbers — profit and value delivered over a period — and a pleasant, deferential subordinate who misses targets is not thereby more loyal; she cites ADOR reaching with a girl group in two years results that top boy bands usually reach in five to seven (her claim).

Describes entertainment as a business made with people rather than inanimate products: it works by moving people's hearts and through people's hearts, so it is volatile — at peak emotion consumers will buy almost anything, allowing steep growth, while a dating rumour or an emotional upset can swing a share price — and handling that risk takes deep, specific know-how.

Rejects handing producing to a 'professional manager': people are swayed by the word 'professional', but expertise means understanding of the field built on years inside it; after twenty years she concluded that producing and management must not be separated, because once split they run on separate tracks and stop meshing.

Explains the May 2024 university-festival run as a long-planned decision serving several aims: fans outside Seoul had no concert to attend yet, students' energy was good for the members, and the group needed live practice before a planned world tour, festival crowds being the closest thing to Lollapalooza or Coachella; anticipating claims that the members were being worked for money, ADOR donated the fees, which come from school budgets; she calls this a choice only a producer who is also the manager can make, because it signals the group's image and direction.

Describes sequencing releases backwards from live plans: with Tokyo Dome in June and a world tour planned for the following year, an album was being prepared for year-end because a world tour needs a secured setlist.

Explains a structural conflict in holding-company groups: affiliates kept in-house for consolidated revenue can lose their edge because work keeps arriving, unlike freelancers who must stay sharp; her rule was to use in-house affiliates first but, under non-exclusive terms, go outside when quality fell short and make in-house and outside teams compete on quality and price — e.g. making goods with LINE Friends for its know-how, shared design understanding and lower unit costs — arguing that better goods sales still end up in group revenue and that a manager must keep the end goal in view while deciding fast enough to avoid short-term losses.

Says she deliberately broke the industry habit of keeping parents at arm's length (meeting them only for contracts and settlements): from the start she talked openly with the members' parents, often for an hour or two about small matters, because with young members misunderstandings multiply and decisions on concerts, schedules, the members' condition and their future cannot be made well without the parents' view; she sees this as the CEO's job, since messages relayed by non-decision-makers breed misunderstanding, and credits it partly for the label's results.

States her vision for the members as 'live happily': having joined young without knowing what an artist is or how the system works, they should use the seven-year contract to learn how to make their own living afterwards — independence rather than spoon-feeding — and be free to choose their path later (to marry or study abroad, for instance); she calls holding artists through renewals for company profit short-sighted, since new teams and markets keep changing.

Says she dislikes K-pop hardening around whatever succeeds, with everyone adopting the winning style: the scene only stays viable if styles keep alternating, and if only her group's style multiplied even her group would struggle; she wanted to show, while making money, that a label which leaves room for others and guarantees autonomy can be a business role model.

Gives a production-economics example: the 'Hurt' video was shot in under an hour during the 'Attention' shoot as face close-ups — what fans love but a lead video cannot carry — and used for the b-side; she says NewJeans' video budgets were below the industry average (four 'Hype Boy' videos for the cost of one) because thinking substituted for spending.

Describes her financial discipline as label head: investment arrives once and the CEO allocates it like a household budget; her motto was to take no further capital and spend as little as possible of what had been received, since she dislikes debt; overseas shoots were practical rather than glamorous — playing unreleased music outdoors in Korea risks leaks — and once abroad they shot many pieces on tight schedules while avoiding night work, which costs more.

Says that earning from people who like you can feel uncomfortable, and that her answer is density of quality: make so many good things that a fan with little money picking blindly still never gets a dud, so spending never feels wasted — this, she says, is her feedback to fans.

claim: Says she designed the May 2024 album hoping it would be enjoyed the way she enjoys old records with outstanding graphics displayed at home, and that fans did exactly that, using the packages as room décor.

Rejects the idea that a broad style such as Y2K can belong to one group: contemporary culture recombines many earlier sources, collaging them through one's own personality — an age of re-creation — so 'it's all mine' claims are untenable; her objection, she says, was to similarity of formula, not to shared styles.

Concedes that a distinctive image inevitably becomes standardised once others absorb it, but argues there is a threshold in how densely it is borrowed — up to a point is acceptable, beyond it crosses a line; she says she watched for a long time before objecting and did not see the objection as serving only her own group.
Describes her meticulousness as selective: she is exacting about aesthetic matters she cares about and has little patience for areas that do not interest her.

Rejecting a producer-only role, says that asking her only to produce shows ignorance of the business — she would not have joined on those terms — and that the work loses its meaning once management and producing are separated.

Criticises the K-pop 'system': in her view a system is what owners build to make employees easy to direct; it does not advance the craft, and schematic, machine-like factory systems are a disease in entertainment.

Recalls ignoring most mainstream Korean pop as a young listener because little of it resonated, so her taste formed as its own category; of the generation that crossed from analogue to digital in their twenties — taping radio songs onto blank cassettes, learning Photoshop as Macs reached her university — she treated a CD as precious, hearing the whole tracklist and reading the booklet until it wore out, and regrets how cheap CDs have become.

Retells joining SM at 25 as the largest company, telling interviewers she came not for love of music but because graphic design was an undeveloped function she could contribute; with no design department she nearly quit in her first year or two, and stayed after producer Lee Soo-man told team leaders by email to follow her lead on graphics despite her junior rank — being backed, she says, made the hardship worth enduring.

Advises that there is no universal method for working with superiors: every boss differs, so each person must build their own know-how for persuading theirs instead of feeling wronged; a company that took you in when you had nothing and tolerated your mistakes is where you learn organisations and society while being paid, and this is easier to learn young; she wishes people came with a manual for how to work with them.

Describes telling the NewJeans members as truthfully as possible how to work well and how the industry runs — in stages, so it hurts less — because the business is not a beautiful one, ignorance is no virtue, and knowing enough builds resilience against later shocks.

Explains routing all money matters, including settlements, through the parents rather than the members to protect their innocence, since handling large sums young erodes it and makes a normal life impossible; she wants them to know how ordinary people their age live, because losing that sense of reality would pull them away from the team she envisioned, and lets them quarrel and make up so they learn how to reconcile.

Says the central question in producing NewJeans was how to keep their natural, innocent feel from debut through promotion: the idols she had seen lived under too many rules — mocked as dolls when compliant, attacked when not — which is too much for teenagers to carry.

Says that to the members she is both the boss and their mothers' age, which keeps a distance however kindly she acts; unlike a mother, a company can feel as if it would dismiss you over a mistake, so she deliberately conveyed that she would never abandon them, whatever they did wrong.

Describes the ADOR tote bag: a parachute-type fabric chosen to have a slight sheen without bulk, priced low but stylish; she wanted to give the audience a new green colourway, but the minimum order quantity and cost were too high.

Says she drew a seven-year picture for NewJeans spanning the whole exclusive-contract period and talked it through with the members; she felt she was clearing it like a series of challenges year by year, was confident each annual album would surprise people if the plan held, and did not want the shared blueprint to turn into false hope for the members.

Describes her business style as not selling: instead of pitching, she makes people as curious as possible ('Min Hee-jin's girl group?', 'what kind of team?'), relying on the trust her past work has earned.

Says she talks to the members as one would to children — 'I liked this kind of music, try it' — without wanting to make them her avatars: each has a clear personality and taste and digests what she offers in her own way; she suspects she was drawn at the auditions to something they had in common with her.

Traces her insistence on integrated control to SM, where as creative director she had no management authority and widened her scope through the work itself; the dilemmas of that period convinced her that realising a vision needs production, upfront investment and management moving together, that choosing what to spend on and what to save is a trade-off, and that cost efficiency creates value — a creator who understands K-pop and maximises management can make more creative work that spreads and grows as a business.
Reported as telling the Da Vinci Motel audience that nobody reaches the top by only following what has already been done, and that the factory-like system has become a disease for the industry.
Announces her resignation from ADOR and departure from HYBE and asks the public to follow the new K-pop venture she will pursue next.

Says leaving trends behind to create trends takes confidence plus a density of finish that leaves no room for rebuttal, and that details carry it: the day before Tokyo Dome the outfit first matched for Hanni's 'Aoi Sangoshō' cover did not work, so she directed a Saint James-style striped top with a white skirt and kitten heels — none were to hand, so a chunky vintage heel was found — because people who knew the song's era would judge every detail.

Says she planned NewJeans with confidence despite plenty of unsolicited advice, believing that something good cannot be refused, and that she dislikes interference when drawing the big picture and setting direction.
Told Nikkei she is wary of K-pop as popular culture becoming isolated and 'Galapagos-like', and wants to bring many kinds of beautiful art into popular culture.

Explains choosing Matsuda Seiko's 'Aoi Sangoshō' for Hanni at Tokyo Dome: as the group's first showcase-like fan meeting in Japan it needed a definite imprint; she loves surprises and wanted an atmosphere not seen among contemporary groups, expecting catharsis when a huge stadium met an unexpected song; she credits Hanni's fit with the song's image and her ability to make it her own.

Says the world tour planned for 2025 was being designed around cultural respect for each host country, with special stages suited to each country, city and venue, aiming to offer something fresh even to people who could not attend.

claim: Details her HYBE headquarters interior: as a designer she preferred private, beautifully partitioned spaces, but an open-plan office was requested, so she added moving racks to screen desks and add storage; she kept the views open to all staff rather than reserving corners for executives, fought for a top-floor specialty-coffee café from a Korean brand as a common rest space, turned down an in-house music-video studio as impractical, and designed nap rooms, showers and a gym with a city view — down to doorknobs and tiles — on a limited budget, choosing inexpensive materials that do not look cheap, as small Japanese capsule hotels do.

Recalls discovering Earth, Wind & Fire by humming a hook to a record-shop owner she trusted — shop owners were heavy listeners whose digging and taste differed shop by shop — who handed her a live album; although she normally prefers clean studio versions and dislikes singers departing from the original, hearing people play live made the studio versions sound flat.
